title: Light as a Switch: EPR Evidence for the Wavelength-Modulated Generation of Intrinsic and Defect-Associated Ti3+ Centers in a MUV-10(Ca) Framework
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Titanium-based metal–organic frameworks (Ti-MOFs) are widely investigated for their potential in photocatalytic applications owing to their unique structural and electronic properties. However, the local identity of long-lived photoinduced Ti(III) species remains unresolved. In this study, the nature of photogenerated Ti(III) species in the stable Ti-MOF MUV-10(Ca) was examined by electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy. The results of X- and Q-band (9/34 GHz) continuous wave (CW) EPR provided unequivocal evidence for the presence of two chemically distinct Ti(III) sites, with the selectivity of Ti(IV) photoreduction governed by the hydration state of the material and the wavelength of the incident light. Consolidation of CW EPR and 1H Davies electron-nuclear double resonance (ENDOR) data allowed us to clearly determine the structure of both centers: one associated with an ideal Ti2Ca2-cluster and another one assigned to the missing-linker defect of the MUV-10(Ca) structure. This first example of such hydration state and wavelength-controlled selectivity in photoactive Ti-MOFs contributes to a deeper understanding of the nature of photoactive centers in Ti-MOFs, highlighting the importance of defect engineering for advanced applications.

title: Hollow Silica Nanoparticles with Tunable Morphology and Porosity
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Hollow silica nanoparticles (HSNPs) are promising nanomaterials for applications such as antireflection coatings, catalysis, and gas separation membranes. Their hollow cores and tunable porosity provide a unique combination of a low refractive index, a high surface area, and selective transport properties. However, precise control of the structure of HSNPs remains challenging because the formation pathways are highly sensitive to synthesis conditions. We systematically examine the influence of poly(acrylic acid) (PAA), tetraethyl orthosilicate (TEOS), and ammonia concentrations on particle morphology to gain insight into the mechanisms governing the formation of HSNPs. Distinct regimes of nanospheres, nanochains, and aggregates are identified, with the core size and shell thickness of nanospheres independently governed by the concentrations of PAA and TEOS. Increasing the PAA/TEOS ratio promotes the formation of nanochains with higher aspect ratios and increased porosity. Elevated ammonia concentrations induce a transition to yolk–shell nanochains by accelerating silica condensation and entrapping sub-10 nm particles within the hollow cores. Applying this mechanistic insight, we extend the approach to fabricate ceria–silica yolk–shell composites. These results highlight a versatile design principle for tailoring HSNP morphology and porosity, providing practical guidelines for scalable synthesis and application across diverse structures.

title: Transport Pathway Engineering in a Three-Terminal Diamond Schottky Photodiode for High-Temperature Dual-Mode Solar-Blind Ultraviolet Detection
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Diamond is promising for solar-blind ultraviolet (SBUV) photodetection in high-temperature extreme environments. However, stable self-powered operation and high-gain response are difficult to reconcile in diamond photodetectors. Photovoltaic diamond photodiodes offer stable zero-bias operation at the expense of limited responsivity, whereas photoconductive-type devices provide gain but often compromise thermal robustness. Here, we introduce transport-pathway engineering in a three-terminal diamond Schottky photodiode to realize dual-mode high-temperature SBUV detection. The device consists of a common Pt/O-terminated diamond Schottky terminal on a single-crystal boron-doped diamond epitaxial platform, together with a backside ohmic terminal and a coplanar ohmic terminal that share the same diamond drift layer. By selecting the carrier-collection terminal, this three-terminal architecture defines either one-dimensional vertical transport (VT) or mixed vertical–lateral transport (VLT) within a unified diamond Schottky photodiode. From 300 to 580 K, the VT pathway supports low dark current, stable self-powered photovoltaic operation with a root-mean-square current fluctuation of 0.81 fA, whereas the VLT pathway enables high-gain biased detection at elevated temperature. Under 215 nm illumination at 580 K, the high-gain detection mode achieves a responsivity of 919.2 A·W–1 at 10 V and a specific detectivity of 7.72 × 1013 Jones under the shot-noise-limited approximation. These results demonstrate that transport-pathway engineering provides a route to complementary self-powered photovoltaic and high-gain biased operating modes in thermally robust diamond Schottky photodiodes for high-temperature optoelectronics.

title: Effect of Filler Conductive Threshold on Cathodic Protection and Anticorrosion Mechanism of Zinc-rich Epoxy Coatings
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract In this study, reduced graphene oxide (rGO) fillers with electrical conductivities spanning nearly five orders of magnitude (4.2 × 10–4 – 20.58 S/cm) were prepared by hydrothermal reduction and incorporated at a fixed loading of 0.5 wt % into zinc-rich epoxy coatings containing 50 wt % zinc powder. The influence of the reduction-dependent rGO state on coating structure, interfacial properties, cathodic protection, and corrosion resistance was systematically evaluated. A non-monotonic conductivity–performance relationship was observed, with rGO160 (1.62 S/cm) showing the best overall protection under the present formulation. XPS and FTIR revealed that rGO160 retained an intermediate surface polarity, while cross-sectional SEM and mechanical tests indicated a dense coating structure, reduced interfacial defects, and the highest pull-off adhesion strength (∼6.4 MPa). KPFM further showed a comparatively uniform contact-potential-difference distribution. After 30 days of immersion, the MZrZE-rGO160 coating retained the highest low-frequency impedance modulus (|Z|0.01Hz ≈ 4 × 107 Ω·cm2) and exhibited the lowest relative corrosion propagation after 300 h of salt-spray exposure. DFT calculations showed comparatively less favorable H2O and O2 adsorption on the idealized rGO160 surface (+0.03 and +0.61 eV, respectively), serving as supplementary thermodynamic descriptors rather than direct kinetic evidence. The results demonstrate that the optimum protection arises from the coupled balance of conductivity, surface chemistry, sheet dispersion/restacking, conductive-network connectivity, and coating integrity. Accordingly, 1.62 S cm–1 should be regarded as a formulation-dependent optimum among the investigated rGO fillers rather than a universal conductivity threshold.

title: Sn/Cl Co-Doped ZnO Cathode Interfacial Layer for High-Performance Organic Photodetectors
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Organic photodetectors (OPDs) hold significant promise for applications spanning medical monitoring, bioimaging and night vision due to their unique advantages, such as flexibility, light weight, and potential for large-area fabrication. Nevertheless, the dark current density (Jd) of OPDs exhibits a pronounced increase under applied reverse bias, which consequently degrades the specific detectivity (D*). To tackle this challenge, this work proposes an interface engineering strategy based on Sn/Cl co-doped ZnO (SCZO). The doping effectively reduces oxygen defects in ZnO, causing the valence band maximum (VBM) to shift downward, thereby suppressing hole injection under bias and reducing Jd. Experiments show that the SCZO-based device exhibits a Jd of 4.05 × 10–11 A cm–2 at –0.1 V, nearly one order of magnitude lower than that of the control device (4.07 × 10–10 A cm–2). Notably, the SCZO-based OPD enables real-time and accurate monitoring of human heart rate, demonstrating its considerable potential for health-monitoring applications. Furthermore, OPDs incorporating the SCZO interface exhibit excellent imaging performance under 820 nm illumination. These findings underscore the significant potential of SCZO-based OPDs for flexible, wearable health monitoring and near-infrared imaging applications.

title: Antimony-Doped Violet Phosphorus Nanosheets: Band Gap Engineering for Enhanced Photodynamic Effect and Efficient Antibacterial Activity
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Bacterial infections pose a severe threat to public health worldwide, and overuse of traditional antibiotics induces bacterial resistance, limiting the efficacy of conventional therapies. Two-dimensional violet phosphorus nanosheets (VPNS) have emerged as promising photodynamic antibacterial materials owing to their unique layered structure and light-responsive capability. However, the inherent wide band gap of VPNS restricts photogenerated electron transition and reactive oxygen species production, resulting in unsatisfactory photodynamic therapy efficiency, which severely hinders their biomedical applications. To address these limitations, a facile antimony (Sb) doping strategy is developed to modulate the electronic band structure of VPNS for significantly boosted photodynamic antibacterial performance. As a congener of phosphorus, Sb possesses excellent optical and electrical properties, which can effectively optimize the photoelectric characteristics of VPNS. Results confirm that Sb doping narrows the band gap of VPNS from 1.91 to 1.42 eV and boosts reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation by 2.3-fold. In mouse skin wound infection models, Sb-doped VPNS (VPSb) achieves remarkable therapeutic efficacy against Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) infection and accelerates wound healing at a low concentration of 0.1 mg/mL. The optimized VPSb, with its excellent therapeutic performance, demonstrates great application prospects for clinical bacterial wound infection therapy.

title: Growth-Controlled Strain-Driven Epitaxial Spalling of Freestanding Oxide Membranes
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Freestanding complex-oxide membranes are promising platforms for heterogeneous integration, strain engineering, and device architectures on non-native substrates. Strain-driven epitaxial spalling offers a sacrificial-layer-free route to such membranes, but its use in complex oxides has so far been explored mainly under fixed growth conditions. Here we show that the formation of freestanding LaAlO3/SrTiO3 micromembranes can be systematically controlled by tuning the pulsed-laser-deposition (PLD) conditions of the LaAlO3 stressor layer. By mapping the membrane formation yield as a function of laser fluence and oxygen background pressure, we identify a process window for reproducible high-yield spalling and correlate it with cracking behavior, membrane release, and microstructural evolution. We show that efficient spalling requires both sufficient elastic-energy accumulation and preservation of a structurally coherent early interface. Low oxygen pressure conditions during the first unit cells as well as low laser fluence during growth promote premature strain relaxation and suppress membrane formation. We also show that, within the optimized growth window, additional perovskite layers can be integrated into the LaAlO3/SrTiO3 architecture while preserving the spalling process, enabling the design of functionalized spalled membranes. We further show that complete spalling, with high-yield membrane formation, is achieved for LaAlO3 thicknesses down to 53–55 nm, substantially reducing the total membrane thickness compared with previous implementations. Finally, we demonstrate that the spalling approach can be extended to selected alternative substrates, including Ca-doped SrTiO3 and Sr2RuO4. These results establish epitaxial spalling as a growth-controlled and interface-sensitive route to structurally complex freestanding oxide micro-membranes.

title: A Molecular-Sieving Pitch Shell Decouples Surface Passivation from Sodium Storage in Hard-Carbon Anodes for Sodium-Ion Batteries
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Pitch carbon coating is a practical route to reconcile the capacity–kinetics trade-off of biomass-derived hard-carbon anodes for sodium-ion batteries, yet the role of the coating sequence has not been isolated. Here, an identical, industrially realistic 2 wt % pitch loading was applied to a lychee-wood hard carbon either before carbonization (co-carbonization, HC-PB) or after it (thin-shell carbonization at 800 °C, HC-PA25), and both were benchmarked head-to-head against the pitch-free baseline. Neither route alters the turbostratic bulk, the 324–328 mAh g–1 first-sodiation capacity, or its plateau/slope partition. Dual-probe (N2/CO2) adsorption shows that the two sequences engineer the pores oppositely. The post-coated shell seals the open surface porosity (N2-accessible area 115 → 3.6 m2 g–1) while retaining the internal ultramicropores, including the whole sub-0.45 nm population (0.068 vs 0.064 cm3 g–1), a molecular-sieving gate, whereas co-carbonization erases that population entirely (its pore-size distribution starts at 0.48 nm) and kinetically gates the rest (40% lower CO2 uptake, pronounced trapping hysteresis). The sieving shell raises the initial Coulombic efficiency to 91.3%, stabilizes an organic-rich solid electrolyte interphase (SEI), and delivers the best long-term cycling stability (237.7 mAh g–1 after 1000 cycles at 5C/2C) while maintaining a high rate capability (259.0 mAh g–1 at 10C desodiation, 88.3% retention). Although co-carbonization gives HC-PB the highest apparent Na+ diffusivity, the decisive advantage of the pitch-after route lies at the interface, and in Na4Fe3(PO4)2P2O7 full cells it translates into 89.6% capacity retention after 200 cycles vs 81.2% for the baseline and only 65.1% for the co-carbonized HC-PB.

title: Fabrication of Microwave-Responsive Confined NaCl in Polydopamine
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Microwave-responsive nanoparticles hold promising applications in microwave thermal therapy and electromagnetic shielding; however, fabricating nanoparticles with high energy conversion efficiency remains challenging. This study leverages the catechol and amino groups in polydopamine (PDA) molecules to achieve simultaneous loading of Na+ and Cl– ions. Through potassium persulfate oxidation to protonate PDA's amino groups for Cl– adsorption, followed by Tris-base pH adjustment to facilitate Na+ binding with catechol groups, we successfully confined sodium chloride (NaCl) within PDA via layer-by-layer assembly, creating highly efficient NaCl@PDA microwave-responsive nanoparticles. Systematic investigation revealed that toluene and potassium persulfate dosage significantly influenced nanoparticle size, with 2 g of potassium persulfate yielding uniform spherical nanoparticles (≈149 nm diameter) with well-defined morphology. Through systematic optimization of the NaCl content, we found that a loading of 36.0 wt % endowed the nanoparticles with exceptional thermal conversion performance under ultralow-power microwave irradiation (2 W, 2450 MHz), achieving 53 °C within 600 s demonstrating 1.7-fold and 1.4-fold faster heating rates compared to physiological saline and pure PDA nanoparticles, respectively. The synthesized nanoparticles exhibit superior microwave responsiveness, showing great potential for applications in microwave thermal therapy and stealth coating technologies.

title: Digitally Printed Gold Nanoelectronics for Tap-to-Detect Electrochemical Biosensing and Chemical Sensing
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Printed electrochemical sensors offer a promising route toward decentralized diagnostics and environmental monitoring, but their practical use remains constrained by complex electrode fabrication and instrument-dependent readout. Here, we present a tap-to-detect sensing platform that couples digitally printed gold nanoparticle nanoelectronics with a battery-free near-field communication (NFC) potentiostat. Single-pass digital materials deposition enables direct fabrication of ready-to-use AuNP working/counter electrodes and AgNP reference electrodes on a flexible polyimide substrate, producing mechanically robust and electrochemically reliable devices. The NFC potentiostat provides smartphone-based wireless voltammetric readout with performance comparable to a commercial potentiostat. As proof of versatility, the printed AuNP electrode is applied to two distinct sensing modes: the thiol-mediated aptamer functionalization enables label-free HER2 biosensing with a detection limit of 4.87 pg mL–1 and successful analysis in spiked human serum, while the intrinsic Au–As interaction enables direct As(III) detection with a detection limit of 42.5 ng mL–1, without additional electrode modification. This digitally printed, smartphone-readable gold nanoelectronic platform provides a scalable pathway toward portable electrochemical sensing for healthcare and environmental applications.

title: Nanoscale Surface Modification of Li6PS5Cl Particles To Stabilize Lithium Solid-State Battery Interfaces
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Thiophosphate solid electrolytes (SEs) may enable the energy storage transformation to solid-state batteries, but interface instability and lithium dendrite formation significantly limit their practical application. To address these challenges, we present a scalable N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) surface modification to boost the performance of Li6PS5Cl (LPSCl) SE. This NMP surface modification on LPSCl improves electrochemical stability of the SE in the positive electrode and stabilizes the lithium-metal interface when used as a separator. When used as SE in positive electrode and separator, the modified LPSCl (m-LPSCl) increases the first cycle discharge capacity by ∼11 mAh g–1 at a current density of 0.21 mA cm–2 and improves capacity retention by 10% over pristine LPSCl (p-LPSCl) after 100 cycles. As a separator, higher critical current density is reached with m-LPSCl (1.6 mA cm–2) than with p-LPSCl (1 mA cm–2) before shorting of the cell. For the pair of single-crystal LiNiO2 (LNO)-positive electrode and lithium metal-negative electrode, m-LPSCl enables over 100 stable cycles, significantly outperforming the cell with p-LPSCl, which shorts after 25 cycles. Overall, this study introduces a scalable method for modifying LPSCl by solvent treatment that improves positive electrode performance and increases stability of the lithium metal-negative electrode interface.

title: Will this sleep-disorder drug be the next big blockbuster?
source: Nature
abstract: Orexin agonists have been approved for the treatment of a type of narcolepsy, yet they could also treat conditions across the health spectrum.

title: Boosting Carrier Mobility and Restoring Ambipolarity in 2D TMD Transistors via Nano-spherical Probe Cleaning
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Two-dimensional (2D) transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), particularly MoS2 and WSe2, are ideal candidates for constructing next-generation high-performance electronics due to their atomic thickness and excellent electrical tunability. However, interface contaminants and bubbles inevitably introduced during device fabrication remain a critical challenge, acting as scattering centers that severely limit carrier mobility and induce device instability. This study demonstrates an in situ mechanical contact strategy using a nano-spherical probe to precisely remove interface residues in MoS2/hBN and WSe2/hBN van der Waals heterostructures. Experimental results indicate that this method significantly reduces interface roughness from ∼11.5 to ∼1.35 nm. The cleaned MoS2 field-effect transistors (FETs) exhibited a significant increase in effective electron mobility from ∼8.5 to 79.2 cm2/V·s, an improvement of approximately one order of magnitude in the on/off ratio, and a significant suppression of charge-trapping-induced hysteresis. For WSe2 devices, the technique successfully restored intrinsic symmetric ambipolar transport characteristics, enhancing both electron and hole drive currents. Furthermore, a 90-day monitoring period in a non-vacuum environment revealed the different degradation mechanisms of interface adsorbates on n-type and p-type carrier transport. This work not only confirms the universality of nanomechanical cleaning technology in enhancing the intrinsic performance of 2D material heterostructure devices but also deeply elucidates the structure–property relationship regarding long-term stability, providing guidance for the interface engineering of high-performance 2D electronics.

title: Butterfly wing patterns make motion hard to read
source: Nature
abstract: Movement can expose camouflaged prey, yet whether colour patterns help moving prey to avoid capture is a long-standing puzzle. Butterfly wings might offer an answer.

title: Increased southward swings of the South Indian convergence zone under greenhouse warming
source: Nature Climate Change
abstract: Extreme southward swings of the South Indian convergence zone can lead to severe rainfall and flooding in southern Africa. Here the authors show that climate change leads to an increase in the frequency and intensity of such swings.

title: High-risk antimicrobial resistance genomic traits in multidrug-resistant Salmonella across China’s food chain: projections to 2050
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is rising globally, yet factors shaping its genomic evolution remain poorly understood. We investigated how socioeconomic, climate, and health factors are associated with AMR spread in multi-drug resistant (MDR) Salmonella enterica across China’s food chain, mapped hotspots and forecasted genomic trait prevalence to 2050. We analysed 2,536 MDR genomes from 15 provinces over 16 years, covering patients, food and non-food workers, meat, livestock, and environmental sources. A machine learning framework integrated genomic surveillance with risk assessment to identify high-risk AMR traits (clinically relevant, MDR, mobile). Regression models linked trait prevalence to socioeconomic, climate, health, and antimicrobial consumption data, informing projections to 2050. Eighty-four high-risk traits, including carbapenem, colistin, and β-lactam resistance, are projected to rise, with antibiotic use, population growth, healthcare spending, and urbanisation. Projections were trait-specific: blaCTX-M-64 and blaTEM-1 may increase up to 20%, while blaCTX-M-65 and blaCTX-M-14 remain below 5%. A mechanistic shift in fluoroquinolone resistance is projected: mutation-based resistance (gyrA 87) declines while plasmid-mediated genes (qnrB17, qnrS1) rise. Food workers emerged as a potential reservoir, showing higher trait prevalence than food sources, uniquely carrying last-resort antibiotic-resistance genes (blaTEM-30, blaNDM-5, blaCTX-M-64). Integrating genomic with socioeconomic surveillance could shift AMR interventions from reactive to preventive.

title: Estimation of aggregate flexibility regions for distributed flexible resources using limited information
source: ScienceDirect Publication: Applied Energy
abstract: Distributed flexible resources (DFRs) can support power-system operation only if aggregators can report their flexibility regions as operating conditions change. Existing aggregation methods generally require detailed device-level states, which may be unavailable, as well as repeated online optimization. This paper proposes a limited-information physics-informed neural network (PINN) for estimating aggregate flexibility regions of DFRs. Its inputs are low-dimensional operating-condition descriptors, and its output is a feasibility-oriented representative polyhedral region conditioned on those descriptors. Physical feasibility and boundary tightness are embedded through support- and projection-based errors and differentiable active-hyperplane residuals, enabling training without precomputed ground-truth flexibility-region labels. The proposed pretraining, full-network training, and loss-weight scheduling scheme prioritizes physical feasibility while retaining boundary tightness. Case studies show that the estimated regions vary predictably with operating conditions and achieve a favorable balance between physical implementability and economic performance relative to alternative aggregation models. Across the operational tests, 96.25% of PINN dispatch trajectories had zero relative disaggregation error, and the maximum error was 4.72%. Dispatch costs remained comparable to those of the full-information inner approximation. Once trained, the estimator requires neither complete device-level information nor an online optimization solver. The proposed framework therefore lowers the deployment barrier for condition-dependent flexibility estimation in practical distributed-resource aggregation.

title: G-quadruplex structures affect the immune response to bacterial infection in mouse macrophages
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Macrophages orchestrate immunity via transcriptional reprogramming, largely controlled by the master regulator NF-κB. However, mechanisms of promoter selection remain enigmatic. Here, we reveal that DNA secondary structures called G-quadruplexes (G4s) modulate the macrophage transcriptome during inflammation. By investigating the G4 ligand pyridostatin (PDS) in lipopolysaccharide-stimulated macrophages, we establish that G4 stabilization significantly decreases the inflammatory response without affecting mitochondrial metabolism or pathogen clearance. Instead, NF-κB-dependent transcription of activation markers and proinflammatory cytokines is selectively repressed. Using chromatin accessibility profiling, NF-κB ChIP, and in silico predictions, we demonstrate that G4 stabilization sterically hinders NF-κB promoter occupancy. Furthermore, PDS stabilizes transient, transcription-induced G4s, prematurely shutting down transcription and reverting local chromatin to a dormant state. Thus, G4 formation represents a potential strategy to modulate dysregulated macrophage activation.

title: Type I IFN promotes ILC2-to-ILC1 plasticity in pre-clinical radiation-induced lung injury
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Radiation-induced lung injury (RILI) is a common dose-limiting toxicity after radiotherapy for lung cancer, but the immunological mechanisms contributing to RILI pathogenesis remain poorly understood. Here we analyze a RILI mouse model using high-dose, restricted-field irradiation to the left lung. Flow cytometry and cytokine profiling analysis of innate lymphoid cells (ILC) reveals a radiation-induced shift from lung-resident type 2 ILCs (ILC2) toward pro-inflammatory type 1 ILCs (ILC1). Single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis of mouse lung ILC populations after radiation suggests that type I interferon (IFN) promotes radiation-induced ILC2-to-ILC1 plasticity. In vitro, IFN-β stimulation of mouse ILC2s leads to increased expression of the ILC1 markers T-bet and IFN-γ, while IFN-β stimulation of human peripheral blood mononuclear cells increases the ILC1-to-ILC2 ratio. In vivo, inhibition of type I IFN signaling attenuates lung damage after irradiation in our RILI model. Thus, our findings indicate that radiation-induced type I IFN induces ILC2-to-ILC1 plasticity to contribute to RILI pathogenesis, and suggest that targeting type I IFN signaling may be a therapeutic strategy to mitigate radiation-induced lung injury.

title: Oncogenic signalling and host immunocompetency govern senescent cell clearance and systemic inflammation in a mouse model of oncogene-induced senescence
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Senescence is a stress-induced program defined by permanent cell-cycle arrest and a pro-inflammatory senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). Defective clearance of senescent cells promotes inflammation, tissue dysfunction, and ageing, yet determinants of their elimination remain poorly understood. Here, we model oncogene-induced senescence in the hematopoietic system by transplanting BrafV600E- or BrafΔN-expressing hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells into recipients with distinct immune backgrounds. BrafV600E induces a stronger senescence program and more aggressive disease than BrafΔN. Survival depends on oncogene-expressing cell burden and host immunity: immunocompetent, lower-burden mice clear oncogene-expressing cells and survive long-term, whereas higher-burden mice show checkpoint upregulation, T-cell exhaustion, and early death. NSG, Rag1KO, and lymphocyte-depleted hosts fail to clear these cells, developing sustained inflammation and bone marrow failure. Rapamycin administration attenuates senescence-associated features and improves survival. These findings identify oncogenic intensity and adaptive immune competence as coupled determinants of senescent-cell fate, with implications for chronic inflammation and senescence-targeted therapies.

title: A prefrontal–bed nucleus pathway controls aversive memory specificity independently of glucocorticoids
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Adaptive memory requires balancing generalization to avoid similar threats with discrimination to recognize safety. The prevailing view is that stress-induced increases in glucocorticoids underlie the enhancement of memory consolidation, strengthening memories and promoting their generalization—referred to here as the standard model. However, circuits that drive memory consolidation often also regulate glucocorticoid release, confounding whether their effects on memory are circuit-driven or hormonally mediated. Here we identify a prefrontal pathway that controls memory specificity independently of glucocorticoids. Using optogenetic manipulations in male rats, we found that post-training inhibition of the rostral prelimbic cortex (rPL) to anteroventral bed nuclei of the stria terminalis (avBST) pathway promoted contextual generalization in an inhibitory avoidance discrimination task without affecting memory strength. Although this manipulation further elevated corticosterone, it produced generalization even in adrenalectomized rats, demonstrating glucocorticoid independence. Conversely, post-training pathway excitation enhanced contextual discrimination. Recordings of calcium signals revealed context-specific engagement of both avBST and avBST-projecting rPL neurons during memory retrieval, with greater responses in the neutral than the aversive context. These findings reveal glucocorticoid-independent circuit control of memory specificity, setting boundary conditions on the standard model and demonstrating mechanistic heterogeneity that may inform stress-related disorders where memory generalization is a core feature.

title: Starting material syntheses for non-aqueous molecular uranium chemistry
source: Chemical Society Reviews
abstract: Various routes to uranium halides, amides and borohydrides which have been developed over the past 75 years are discussed with a focus on their use as synthetic access to uranium starting materials in the oxidation states +III to +VI.

title: Development of bio-based flame-retardant polyurethane
source: Chemical Society Reviews
abstract: Bio-based, low-toxicity flame-retardant polyurethane supports sustainability through renewable biomass, molecular engineering, circular economy, and advanced design to reduce environmental impacts. (Icons generated by Google Nano Banana 2).

title: Divergent anaerobic fates of biodegradable plastics in landfill leachate
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Biodegradable plastics (BPs) are increasingly promoted as sustainable alternatives to conventional polymers, yet their fate in landfills remains poorly understood. Here, we evaluated the anaerobic biodegradability of three BPs, polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB), poly(lactic acid) (PLA), and poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT), in landfill leachate under mesophilic conditions by quantifying carbon conversion to biogas. The BPs exhibited sharply contrasting degradation trajectories: PHB mineralized completely within 17 d, whereas PLA underwent substantial mineralization over 320 d (83.6%), extending beyond the well-established expectation of limited mesophilic degradation. In contrast, PBAT remained largely recalcitrant. Multi-omics analyses linked PHB and PLA depolymerization to the biofilm–polymer interface, with depolymerase transcription tracking their distinct degradation phases. Putative depolymerase homologs were widespread across recovered bacterial genomes, yet only a subset showed transcriptional support. This active fraction included multiple under-characterized lineages outside the taxonomic range of experimentally validated degrader genomes, revealing a marked disconnect between genomic potential and realized activity. Our findings show that anaerobic biodegradation outcomes in landfill leachate cannot be inferred from biodegradability labels or genomic potential alone, but emerge from polymer-specific depolymerization constraints and depolymerase transcription enriched at the biofilm–polymer interface.

title: Fatty acids in the tumor microenvironment reprogram neutrophils to induce adenosine-mediated immunosuppression in mice
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: As solid tumors progress, the tumor microenvironment becomes increasingly immunosuppressive, impairing cytotoxic T-cell activity and limiting the efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade. However, the mechanistic drivers of this immunosuppression remain poorly understood. Here, we identify a tumor-derived lipid–neutrophil–adenosine axis as a critical regulator of immune suppression in advanced colorectal cancer (CRC). We show that fatty acids enriched in tumor interstitial fluid reprogram neutrophils toward an immunosuppressive phenotype through PPARα activation, upregulation of CD39 and CD73, and adenosine generation, ultimately leading to T-cell suppression. AB928, a dual A2aR/A2bR adenosine receptor antagonist currently in clinical trials, restores T-cell proliferation, effector function, and tumor-killing capacity in vitro and in vivo. Importantly, AB928 synergizes with anti-PD-1 therapy to enhance survival in an immunotherapy-resistant autochthonous model of metastatic CRC. Thus, our findings define a metabolic immune evasion mechanism in the microenvironment and provide a rationale for targeting neutrophil-derived adenosine signaling to improve immunotherapy responses in CRC.

title: Human hemoglobin protects the parasite cytoskeleton during Plasmodium falciparum gametocyte development
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Transmission of Plasmodium falciparum requires the differentiation of asexual parasites into male and female gametocytes, which undergo extensive cytoskeletal remodeling, assembling a non-canonical subpellicular microtubule (SPMT) network. Using single-particle cryo-electron microscopy, we determined structures of SPMTs isolated from developing gametocytes. Unexpectedly, we identified human hemoglobin as a prominent microtubule-associated factor that binds to P. falciparum SPMTs in a dimeric form rather than the canonical tetramer. Pharmacological perturbation of microtubules and hemoglobin isoform switching experiments demonstrate that this hemoglobin-SPMT association is essential for proper SPMT organization and gametocyte maturation. Together, these findings reveal a strategy by which P. falciparum repurposes a host metabolic protein to stabilize its cytoskeleton, highlight the intimate co-evolution between parasite and host, and suggest avenues to block malaria transmission.

title: Targeting high-value uses to unlock the mitigation potential of clean hydrogen
source: Nature Climate Change
abstract: Clean hydrogen is a versatile decarbonization option, but given its energy-intensive production, high costs and limited near-term supply, uses with the greatest environmental and economic benefits must be prioritized. Analysis of ten end-use sectors identifies high-value applications and suggests that uniform supply-side subsidies risk misallocating clean hydrogen and public funds, highlighting the need for sector-specific demand-side policies.

title: Anterior cingulate input tunes striatal dynamics for context-dependent social preference in a mouse model of autism
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Social preference in autism spectrum disorder varies across contexts, but the underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear. Here we show that Shank3 knockout (KO) mice, an autism mouse model, exhibit reduced preference for social over nonsocial stimuli while retaining a preference for females over males. Calcium imaging reveals context-dependent differences between KO and wild-type (WT) mice in the organization of neuronal population dynamics in the dorsomedial striatum (DMS), corresponding to their behavioural preferences. Functional imaging and molecular analyses reveal reduced functional connectivity between the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and DMS and molecular alterations more pronounced in the striatal matrix. ACC inhibition eliminates genotype-dependent differences in DMS dynamics. Inhibiting the ACC–DMS pathway impairs social preference, whereas its activation in KO mice shifts DMS dynamics towards WT patterns and improves social preference. These findings identify a cortical pathway that shapes striatal population dynamics and context-dependent social preference in an autism mouse model.

title: Genes take control of active matter
source: Nature Materials
abstract: Gene expression reconstituted outside the cell controls the composition and dynamics of cytoskeletal networks, bringing the tools of synthetic biology to active matter and opening a route to genetically programmed biomaterials.

title: Production of abundant defective viral genomes by an insect-specific alphavirus revealed by nanopore sequencing
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Defective viral genomes (DVGs) shape virus-host interactions and evolution, yet remain poorly characterized in insect-specific viruses. Using Nanopore direct RNA sequencing (DRS), we profile full-length RNA species of Eilat virus (EILV), a mosquito-restricted alphavirus. We found that EILV produces abundant deletion-type DVGs far exceeding those seen in related arboviruses under identical conditions. These DVGs retain intact terminal sequences with conserved junction motifs. A modified DRS approach reveals widespread premature termination during EILV genomic RNA synthesis, linking DVG formation to reduced replicase processivity. Notably, a subset of DVGs is selectively replicated and packaged, accumulating over serial passages and interfering with parental virus replication. Our findings uncover an intrinsic, high DVG-generating capacity in EILV, linking low-processivity RNA synthesis with increased genomic plasticity. This suggests that elevated DVG production may be an adaptive mechanism, providing important insights into alphavirus evolution and replication fidelity in insect-specific RNA viruses.

title: The Emirati pangenome featuring a diploid chromosome-level reference
source: Scientific community and society : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Reference genomes are essential for identifying and representing human genomic variation, yet single-genome sequences fail to capture population-specific diversity. We present the Emirati pangenome comprising a trio-based, diploid chromosome-level assembly from deep, multi-platform sequencing data and 57 additional high-quality HiFi sequencing-based chromosome-scale assemblies, 27 of which are trio-based. Haplotypes demonstrate high contiguity (median N50 of 151.9 Mb) and good base accuracy (median QV score of 59.31). Of all assembled chromosomes, 31.8% are telomere-to-telomere (T2T) scaffolds (chromosome-spanning sequences flanked by telomeric repeats at both ends), and 64.3% achieved chromosome-level continuity (single scaffolds spanning an entire chromosome but retaining one or more sequence gaps or lacking a telomeric signature at one or both ends). These assemblies form the foundation of the population-specific pangenome graph of the Emirati Reference Genome Project (ERGP), which captures genomic variation comparable to the globally diverse HPRC reference graph, while covering regionally enriched variation. Applying the ERGP pangenome to short‑read genotyping of an independent Emirati cohort revealed structural variant sites in linkage disequilibrium with phenotype‑associated GWAS variants, demonstrating the value of population-graph-based variant inference. The ERGP reference complements human pangenomes and provides a critical foundation for population-specific genomics and precision medicine in the United Arab Emirates.

title: Global green hydrogen site suitability and cost competitiveness: an open-source geospatial and uncertainty assessment across 182 countries
source: ScienceDirect Publication: Applied Energy
abstract: Green hydrogen facility siting is commonly guided either by techno-economic cost minimization or by multi-criteria suitability assessment, yet the extent to which these approaches identify the same development priorities remains unclear. A site that can produce low-cost green hydrogen may not necessarily be suitable. Here, we develop an open-source, spatially explicit framework covering 182 countries that applies both approaches independently to a common technically eligible land base. The framework's methodological novelty lies in independently applying cost minimization and multi-criteria suitability assessment to a common eligible land base, enabling a consistent spatial comparison of cost-optimal and highly suitable locations while integrating spatial exclusions, hourly solar and wind generation modelling, plant-gate levelized cost of hydrogen estimation, spatial water-supply pathways, and Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis. Spatial exclusions reduce globally eligible land to 40%. Solar is the least-cost option across 81% of eligible areas, whereas wind-dominated locations achieve a lower median hydrogen cost of $2.8/kg compared with $3.1/kg for solar. However, it was demonstrated that the lowest-cost locations do not consistently coincide with the highest-suitability areas. These findings show that cost competitiveness and development suitability are related but non-equivalent, and that their combined assessment provides a more robust basis for prioritizing large-scale green hydrogen production.

title: Revealing inter-cell water-gas-coupled transfer characteristics and degradation-driven evolution within large-scale fuel cell stacks
source: ScienceDirect Publication: Applied Energy
abstract: Hydrophobicity decay is a critical driving force behind the degradation of proton exchange membrane fuel cells. However, the cross-scale linkage between microscopic material-level hydrophobic degradation and macroscopic stack-level water-gas transfer behaviors remains largely obscure, as well as the further inducing consequences. Bridging the gap, this study reveals the inter-cell water-gas-coupled transfer characteristics and degradation-driven evolution within large-scale fuel cell stacks. Applying the micro-current excitation method on a 60-cell stack, the evolution of membrane electrode assembly (MEA) material states is recognized after the 1000-h durability test. Except for typical catalyst degradation, an anomalous degradation feature is captured, wherein hydrophobicity degradation facilitates internal water accumulation and reduces ohmic resistance, consequently leading to the performance rise in ohmic polarization region. The degradation inconsistency within stack is found to be correlated with flow maldistribution. At the inter-cell level, cells with lower flow rates suffer from more severe degradation due to water accumulation and potential air starvation, which is especially pronounced in end cells. At the intra-cell in-plane level, the hydrophobicity degradation of MEA at the air downstream region is also more serious. For stacks assembled with MEAs with different hydrophobic states driven by degradation, the internal water accumulation difference and inter-cell coupling effect combine to cause gas redistribution. The evolution of gas distribution with humidity clearly indicates that the tendency of water accumulation within degraded cells increases the flow resistance and decreases the flow rate under high humidity conditions. Consequently, degraded MEAs suffer a greater risk of water flooding and significant deterioration in dynamic response performance, which forms a vicious cycle of accelerated degradation. This study enriches the cross-scale degradation mechanism theory of fuel cell stacks and holds significant values for consistency guarantee and lifetime extension.

title: Large-scale proteomic characterization reveals clinically relevant subtypes of early-stage papillary thyroid cancer for prognostic prediction
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Papillary thyroid cancer (PTC) has a rising incidence. The majority are diagnosed at an early stage, albeit with a minority exhibiting aggressive tendencies. Given its generally indolent nature, controversy persists regarding the management of early-stage PTCs, particularly surgical intervention and long-term surveillance strategies. Here, we conduct a large-scale proteomic characterization of early-stage PTC based on tumor samples from 797 patients. Proteomic profiling unveils clinically relevant modules and identifies six subtypes, capturing the spectrum of heterogeneity from indolent to progressive disease states. Notably, subtypes associated with higher progression risk display enhanced signatures of ribogenesis and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Furthermore, integrating machine learning with protein co-expression network analysis, we identify predictive markers of PTC progression risk such as GPX3 and TMSB4X. Integration of clinical and proteomic data provides a valuable resource for a deeper understanding of early-stage PTC biology and may inform personalized management strategies for patients with indolent or progressive disease.

title: Beyond nature: charting the roadmap to intelligent biomanufacturing for sustainable biohydrogen
source: ScienceDirect Publication: Applied Energy
abstract: Hydrogen has been recognized as a key pillar of future energy systems in the global pursuit of carbon neutrality. However, hydrogen production processes still highly rely on fossil fuels. Biohydrogen production is a microbial-based process that converts biomass, organic waste, and solar energy into hydrogen via dark fermentation, photo-fermentation, or photolytic water-splitting pathways. It is a promising pathway to sustainable energy, with the potential for carbon-negative emissions under favorable feedstock and system-boundary conditions. Yet, the limitations of natural biological systems, such as poor energy conversion efficiency, huge carbon diversion, and poor operational robustness, have prevented its transition from laboratory research to industrial application. To resolve these bottlenecks, this review proposes a strategic shift from traditional biological conversion toward intelligent biomanufacturing via three enabling technologies: (1) synthetic biology to design microbial cell factories with a tailored hydrogen-centric metabolism; (2) nanomaterials engineering to create smart biotic-abiotic interfaces for overcoming the physical limitations of electron and mass transfer; and (3) artificial intelligence to enable autonomous bioprocessing through predictive digital twins and self-optimizing reactor systems. These three pillars can bridge molecular-scale engineering to system-level intelligence. A scalable roadmap starting from modular bioreactor design, waste-derived feedstock integration, and rigorous techno-economic and life-cycle assessment has been outlined to position biohydrogen within circular economy and potentially carbon-negative ecosystems. This review suggests a pathway to make biohydrogen an important, efficient, cost-effective, and reliable building block of the future hydrogen economy.

title: Nutrient stress-driven ACSS1 controls metabolic flexibility and bone formation
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Metabolic dysregulation under nutrient stress disrupts bone homeostasis. Although acetate metabolism is linked to diabetes and alcoholism, its role in the skeletal complications of these conditions remains unknown. Here we identify acetyl-CoA synthetase 1 (ACSS1) as a key stress responder that mediates mitonuclear communication in bone marrow skeletal stem cells. ACSS1-driven rewiring of acetate metabolism impairs cellular metabolic flexibility, mitochondrial function, and osteogenesis. Mechanistically, nutrient excess from glucose, alcohol or acetate upregulates ACSS1 via a mitochondrial ROS activated integrated stress response-CEBPB pathway. Maladaptive ACSS1 accumulation enforces excessive acetyl-CoA production from either exogenous or glucose/ethanol-derived endogenous acetate, promoting mitochondrial protein hyperacetylation specifically inactivating ME2 via lysine 94 acetylation. This ACSS1-triggered ME2 inactivation disturbs the malate-aspartate shuttle, leading to a self-perpetuating cycle of redox imbalance and oxidative stress that exacerbates mitochondrial dysfunction and osteogenic impairment. Importantly, genetic deletion of Acss1 or AAV-delivered non-acetylatable ME2 mutant in osteoprogenitor cells restores mitochondrial resilience, osteogenic capacity, and bone formation, protecting against osteoporosis or osteonecrosis in male mouse models of type 2 diabetes and chronic alcohol consumption. These results unveil an essential role for ACSS1 in controlling metabolic flexibility and osteogenesis, identifying ACSS1 as a potential therapeutic target for metabolic stress-related bone disorders.

title: Peripheral glia drive the initiation of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Although tumor innervation is known to promote cancer progression, underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood and have mostly been linked to axonal signaling. Here, we identify peripheral glia as critical drivers of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC), the second most common skin cancer in humans. Tumor-associated glial cells (TAGs) resemble embryonic Schwann cell lineage stages, are abundant in the stroma of premalignant lesions and established murine and human cSCC, and are essential for tumor formation. TAG activation in premalignant lesions is triggered by UV-induced anti-inflammatory macrophages, which in turn are polarized by TAGs into pro-tumorigenic FcεRIα⁺ macrophages, key components of the cSCC microenvironment. Consequently, TAG depletion reduces FcεRIα⁺ macrophages, cancer-associated fibroblasts, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition in keratinocytes, thereby impairing cSCC initiation by disrupting intercellular communication required for tumor development. As most solid tumors are innervated and harbor peripheral glia, our findings reveal TAGs as regulators of tumor initiation with potential relevance beyond skin cancer.

title: Three-photon population imaging of subcortical brain regions
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Monitoring large-scale neuronal activity in deep brain circuits is crucial for understanding the principles of brain function. However, existing large-scale cellular-resolution imaging techniques are limited in imaging depth and cannot monitor activity in areas deeper than the cortex in the intact brain. To address this challenge, we developed a Large Imaging Field of view Three-photon (LIFT) microscope with a FOV of > 3 mm2. LIFT combines high-numerical-aperture optimized sampling, using a custom scanning module, with deep learning-based denoising, to enable population imaging in subcortical brain regions of mice and deep cortical regions of rats. We demonstrate calcium imaging in the intact mouse brain from more than 1500 cells across CA1, the surrounding white matter, and adjacent deep layers of the cortex, and show population imaging with high SNR at a depth of 1.2 mm in the rat cortex. The LIFT microscope offers versatility in imaging scale and rate and was built entirely from off-the-shelf components.

title: Identification and genetic characterization of megabase-scale plasmids of Enterobacteriaceae
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Humans and animals are ubiquitously colonized by Enterobacteriaceae, including both commensals and clinically significant pathogens. Here, we report 21 complete Enterobacteriaceae megaplasmid genomes of up to 1.58 Mbp in length spanning two major clades that are highly divergent from previously described plasmids. Of these, three were reconstructed from isolates of Escherichia coli and Shigella flexneri; others were potentially hosted by species of Citrobacter and Enterobacter. Related megabase-scale plasmids were detected in at least 400 infant and adult gut, and other microbiomes. Diverse Enterobacteriaceae hosts, conjugation machinery, and DNA modification patterns suggest that these elements are self-transmissible, with a broad host range. The plasmids encode multi-drug efflux systems and potential secreted effectors. Up to 208 tRNAs are encoded and include sequence variants that may counter tRNA-centric defense mechanisms. Overall, the vast plasmid coding capacity may broaden host range, increase competitiveness, control invasion by other elements, and counter programmed cell death.

abstract: Augmented vision sensors preserve high scene fidelity while substantially reducing the data volume with an event-driven data form, thus achieving an effective temporal resolution of ~10 μs.

title: Strong field spectroscopy of many-body interactions in solids
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: High-order harmonic generation (HHG) in solids offers a promising route to compact ultrafast sources of quantum light, but its efficiency and coherence are limited by ultrafast dephasing of laser-driven electron–hole polarization. Although widely described by a phenomenological coherence time, the microscopic origin of this dephasing has remained unresolved. Here, we combine wavelength-dependent HHG measurements in monolayer and bulk semiconductors with ab initio many-body calculations of electron–phonon scattering and strong-field simulations. We show that the measured wavelength scaling of the HHG yield is quantitatively reproduced only when semiconductor Bloch equations incorporate momentum-dependent dephasing derived from first principles scattering rates. The calculations reveal that strong-field-driven carriers rapidly enter regions of the Brillouin zone with enhanced electron–phonon scattering, giving rise to effective few-femtosecond dephasing. Our results establish a microscopic foundation for dephasing in solid-state HHG and provide a framework for engineering coherence in strongly driven solids for quantum photonic applications.

title: Coordinated operation of Mobile substations and multiple Mobile flexible resources in coupled power distribution and transportation networks
source: ScienceDirect Publication: Applied Energy
abstract: To address spatiotemporal load imbalance, temporary capacity shortages, and the limited scheduling potential of grid-side flexibility resources in distribution systems, a coordinated operation method for multi-type mobile flexible resources (MFRs), including mobile substations (MSSs), mobile energy storage systems (MESSs), and mobile diesel generators (MDGs), is proposed in coupled power distribution and transportation networks. First, a coordinated scheduling framework integrating the discrete migration behavior of MFRs with distribution network operation is established. Then, a discrete migration model is developed in the spatial dimension by considering travel and parking states, transportation network accessibility, and the coupling between docking operations and capacity expansion. In the temporal dimension, an installation–disassembly sequential state transition model for MSSs is proposed to characterize the operating states of mobile resources over long-term scheduling horizons. Based on the proposed framework and models, the complementary response characteristics of MSSs, MESSs, and MDGs are coordinated under mobility and network operating constraints. Finally, simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method alleviates spatiotemporal load imbalance and local capacity shortages, improves voltage profiles and system resilience, and provides additional support for PV accommodation under capacity-constrained conditions.

title: Exploring healthy aging through preclinical Alzheimer disease in the Knight Alzheimer Research Imaging dataset
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Alzheimer disease (AD) remains a significant global public health challenge, requiring robust multimodal datasets to elucidate its prolonged preclinical phase, improve early detection, advance understanding of disease trajectories, and guide intervention strategies. Here we present the Knight Alzheimer Research Imaging (KARI) dataset, established by the Washington University Knight ADRC to address this critical need. We detail comprehensive multimodal neuroimaging from 1,645 participants (aged 42-97) across 6,217 acquisitions. Spanning the AD spectrum from healthy aging to symptomatic disease, the cohort undergoes extensive longitudinal imaging using structural and functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) alongside positron emission tomography (PET) tracers for amyloid and tau pathology. This is complemented by rich clinical, cognitive, genetic, and biomarker data. In addition to raw imaging, the dataset provides quality-controlled processed outputs, including anatomical segmentations and biomarker quantification. By making this data accessible to researchers, the Knight ADRC aims to accelerate discoveries in pathophysiology, biomarker identification, and therapeutic development.

title: Interface Engineering in Perovskite Light-Emitting Diodes: Fundamentals, Characterization, Strategies, and Applications
source: Chemical Reviews: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Interface engineering has emerged as a critical strategy for advancing perovskite light-emitting diodes (PeLEDs), enabling remarkable improvements in the device efficiency, stability, and spectral purity. This Review provides a comprehensive overview of interface engineering in PeLEDs, beginning with the fundamental principles that govern carrier injection, transport, and recombination at heterojunctions between perovskite emitters and charge-transport layers. We then survey advanced characterization techniques, including photoelectron spectroscopy, scanning probe microscopy, and time-resolved optical methods, that elucidate interfacial energy-level alignment, defect states, charge dynamics, and degradation pathways. On the basis of these insights, we systematically discuss versatile engineering strategies, such as self-assembled monolayers, dipole interlayers, dimensional regulation, and passivation schemes, to mitigate non-radiative recombination, balance charge fluxes, and enhance operational stability. Finally, we highlight emerging applications spanning high-resolution displays, flexible lighting, and lasing while outlining key challenges and future directions toward commercial realization. This Review aims to offer a holistic framework linking interfacial design to device performance, guiding next-generation PeLED development.

title: Tuning Interfacial Electron Transfer for Boosting Electrochemiluminescence: Methods, Mechanisms, and Bioanalytical Applications
source: Chemical Reviews: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The interfacial electron-transfer process acts as a pivotal kinetic determinant of electrochemiluminescence (ECL) efficiency, governing the generation of excited-state emitters and thus dictating the intensity and stability of ECL signals. Currently, harnessing diverse nanomaterials has driven significant advances in the development of novel ECL luminophores and the activation of coreactants. However, most of these luminophores exhibit low ECL efficiency in aqueous media, and the intrinsic reaction and activation mechanisms remain ambiguous because of their complex structures and compositions. Notably, tuning electron-transfer pathways at the molecular/atomic level can not only enable efficient signal amplification but also facilitate the tracking of reaction pathways, thereby providing deeper insights into the fundamental mechanisms underlying ECL processes. This Review comprehensively summarizes advances during the past five years in tuning interfacial electron transfer to enhance ECL. Furthermore, we highlight progress in electron-transfer-mediated signal amplification strategies for highly sensitive ECL biosensing and bioimaging applications. Finally, we propose and discuss the challenges and perspectives associated with improving the ECL efficiency through the modulation of electron transfer processes. Precise regulation of interfacial electron transfer holds substantial promise for advancing ECL theories, clarifying reaction mechanisms, and expanding the scope of ECL-based bioanalytical applications.

title: Supramolecular chemical ligation of helical polymers
source: Nature Nanotechnology
abstract: Chemical ligation of polymer segments is an essential approach to extend the length of synthetic polymers. Ligating individual polymer chains at the molecular level remains a formidable challenge owing to the entropically disfavoured collision probability between reactive end groups, and the need to overcome the activation barrier. Here we report a pathway to chemical ligation of synthetic polymers via folding-driven supramolecular polymerization followed by dynamic covalent polycondensation. Our strategy, which does not require thermal activation, uses hydrogen bonds that induce conformational folding to rigidify the polymer backbone while providing sticky ends for supramolecular pre-organization. This promotes base-catalysed covalent exchange between terminal groups (in our case, thiolate-disulfide groups). We obtain mechanistic insight in the ligation process by engineering side-chain units that determine conformational foldability and intermolecular H-bonding pre-organization. The resulting extended helical polymers fold into hierarchical globular architectures in solution and exhibit thermo-responsive macromolecular entanglements in bulk films. The combination of noncovalent assembly and dynamic covalent polymerization offers a supramolecular pathway for non-thermal and controllable polycondensation of dynamic polymers with secondary structures.

title: Stacking-specific two-dimensional In2Se3 for ferroelectric homojunctions
source: Nature Nanotechnology
abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) ferroelectric semiconductors offer unique opportunities for ultrathin non-volatile memory and neuromorphic devices, yet the role of stacking order in intrinsic ferroelectric systems remains largely unexplored. Here we report the stacking-controlled growth of large-area 2D β'- and α-In2Se3 with distinct 2H and 3R configurations through chemical vapour deposition by regulating selenium kinetics and strain relaxation. By combining atomic-resolution microscopy, non-linear optical characterization and first-principles calculations, we uncover a strong correlation between stacking order and ferroelectric behaviour: β'-In2Se3 undergoes an antiferroelectric-to-paraelectric transition when switching from 2H to 3R stacking, whereas in α-In2Se3, in-plane ferroelectric polarization vanishes during the 3R-to-2H transition. We further achieve the controlled synthesis of 2H/3R ferroelectric homojunctions and directly visualize polarization-dependent interfacial potential barriers using differential phase-contrast scanning transmission electron microscopy. The engineered homojunctions exhibit switchable band alignment and tunable carrier transport, yielding memristors with significantly reduced switching voltages and an on/off ratio of ∼2.6 × 104, approximately one order of magnitude higher than devices based on single-stacking α-In2Se3. These findings establish stacking order as a powerful structural parameter for tailoring ferroelectricity in 2D materials and introduce stacking-engineered polymorphic heterogeneity as a versatile platform for high-performance ferroelectric electronics and memory technologies.

title: Directed assembly of cathode interlayers enables efficient binary organic solar cells
source: Nature Energy
abstract:
Abstract
                  Cathode interlayers create interfacial dipoles in organic solar cells to maximize device efficiency. However, the dipoles are highly dependent on the molecular orientation of the interlayers, which remain challenging to be controlled. Here, based on the amphiphilic nature of the interlayers, we show a stepwise film deposition approach using a polar solvent for active layer pretreatment and a bipolar solvent for subsequent interlayer self assembly. Sum-frequency generation vibrational spectroscopy reveals a preferred perpendicular orientation of the interlayer molecules, thereby enhancing the surface potential and reducing the charge transport resistance. As a result, we achieve a certified efficiency of 20.65% and fill factor of 82.7% in binary organic solar cells. This method is universally applicable to different cathode interlayers and active layers. Our work highlights the importance of controlling interlayer molecular orientation for unlocking significant performance gains, paving the way for further advancements in device optimization.

title: Continuous health monitoring of solid oxide electrolyzers using pulse-width modulation current interrupt analysis
source: ScienceDirect Publication: Applied Energy
abstract: As solid oxide electrolyzer (SOE) technology moves from button cells to commercial stacks, there is a growing need for fast and inexpensive methods to track the stack’s state-of-health during operation. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) is the standard diagnostic at the lab scale, but the cost, current limitations, and test duration of frequency-response analyzers make routine EIS measurements impractical for large stacks/systems. To address this problem, pulse-width modulation is combined with current-interrupt analysis (PWM-CI) to achieve continuous, in-situ monitoring of SOE health. The proposed PWM-CI method utilizes the “off” portion of the PWM cycle (when the applied voltage to the cell is removed) to perform rapid current interrupt measurements and analyzes the resulting voltage transients using a developed state-space model that explicitly accounts for cable inductance, switch capacitance, and oscilloscope properties. A fitting framework is developed that extracts ohmic, polarization, and total resistances from individual interrupts using only 50 ms of voltage decay, while avoiding the multi-minute interruption of hydrogen production required for EIS. PWM-CI tracking of button cells over 500 h generates ohmic resistances and time constants in agreement with EIS and distribution-of-relaxation-times analysis respectively, and accurately captures the degradation trends. The PWM-CI method is further demonstrated on a 45-cell commercial technology demonstrator stack, where inductive and capacitive effects cause oscillatory transients that are accounted for using the state-space model. After calibration of the electronic parasitics, PWM-CI yields stable resistance and time-constant estimates over 957 h of stack operation. The developed PWM-CI approach provides a practical pathway toward continuous health monitoring of SOE stacks under realistic dynamic operating conditions.

title: Epithelial NF-κB shapes protective Treg cell responses to restrain intestinal inflammation
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Inflammation resolution depends on coordinated communication between tissue compartments, yet how the intestinal epithelium shapes its immune microenvironment remains poorly understood. Here, using colonic biopsies from patients with ulcerative colitis (UC) and mouse models enabling tissue-wide visualization of NF-κB activity, we combine single-cell RNA sequencing and secretome analysis to define epithelial communication during colitis. We show that, paradoxically, the NF-κB-driven pro-inflammatory secretome of intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) is essential for recovery and prevents unrestrained inflammation. Mechanistically, epithelial NF-κB promotes CCL22-dependent regulatory T cell (Treg cell) recruitment and promotes a tolerogenic, pro-repair cell state, accompanied by induction of the lipid-metabolism-associated GDPD3 and CCR4. In UC, epithelial NF-κB is not uniformly activated but instead induces a selective pro-inflammatory transcriptional program while repressing targets regulating T cell recruitment. Thus, we identify dynamic epithelial–immune communication and demonstrate a protective IEC NF-κB–Treg cell axis important for resolution of intestinal inflammation.

title: Macroporous Interlayers Stabilize Long-Lived Hole Polarons in Organic Semiconductor Photoanodes
source: ACS Energy Letters: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Integrating alternative oxidation reactions (AORs) into photoelectrochemical (PEC) systems is promising for unassisted hydrogen production and value-added chemical synthesis, yet organic semiconductor (OS) photoanodes suffer from poor charge extraction and short carrier lifetimes. Here, we address this bottleneck by stabilizing long-lived hole polarons through macroporous tin oxide (mcSnO2) interlayers. Transient absorption spectroscopy reveals that accelerated electron extraction through mcSnO2 stabilizes hole polaron states, substantially prolonging carrier lifetimes. Consequently, the optimized organic photoanodes outperform bare counterparts by more than 5.5-fold, retaining 74% of their initial photocurrent over 15 h for iodide oxidation and 61% over 35 h for ascorbic acid oxidation. Furthermore, integrating this robust organic photoanode with an OS-based photocathode enables the first bias-free organic PEC tandem cell coupling hydrogen evolution with AORs, delivering a remarkable solar-to-hydrogen conversion efficiency of 1.4%. These findings establish interfacial carrier lifetime engineering as an effective strategy for realizing high-performance and durable organic PEC systems.

title: Charge-Density-Dependent Ionomer Effects in Pure-Water CO2 Electrolysis
source: ACS Energy Letters: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Pure-water membrane electrode assemblies (MEAs) represent a promising strategy to eliminate (bi)carbonate salt precipitation for electrochemical CO2 reduction (CO2R). However, the absence of alkali metal cations fundamentally restricts CO2 activation and intermediate stabilization, thereby reducing catalytic performance. Here, we overcome this limitation by identifying the ionomer charge density as a key molecular-level parameter associated with pure-water CO2R. By comparing anion-exchange ionomers with varying charge characteristics, we reveal that high-charge-density ionomer (HCDI) introduces a favorable catalyst–membrane interfacial environment, enabling superior macroscopic CO2R performance. HCDI-enabled MEAs achieve >99% CO Faradaic efficiency at 100 mA cm–2 and sustain ∼92% at 1000 mA cm–2. In situ diagnosis and electrochemical characterization reveal that the HCDI-functionalized interface produces a substantial *CO signal, while concurrently suppressing hydrogen evolution. By decoupling cation effects from liquid electrolytes, these findings support interfacial ionomer charge density as a useful comparative parameter for pure-water CO2 MEA electrolyzers.
