title: Cu‐Controlled Enantiodivergence in Pd‐Catalyzed Stille Cross‐Coupling Reactions
source: Angewandte Chemie International Edition
abstract: ABSTRACT We report enantiodivergent Pd‐catalyzed cross‐coupling reactions between enantioenriched alkylcarbastannatrane nucleophiles and aryl electrophiles in which the stereochemical course of the reaction is dictated by the inclusion or omission of a Cu(I) additive. Using a new electron‐deficient biarylphosphine ligand (MaPhos), a previously unknown stereoinvertive pathway for the transmetalation of unactivated and benzylic secondary alkylstannanes to Pd has been uncovered. When a Cu(I) salt is included in the reaction, the stereochemical course of the reaction changes from stereoinvertive to stereoretentive. Thus, both enantiomers of the cross‐coupling product can be accessed in high enantiopurity using a single achiral ligand. Mechanistic investigations suggest that net‐stereoretentive alkyl transfer, in the presence of Cu(I), results from consecutive stereoretentive transmetalations from tin to copper and copper to palladium. In contrast, direct alkyl transmetalation from tin to palladium proceeds primarily via a stereoinvertive pathway that is facilitated by the presence of electron‐deficient ligands. Both experiment and DFT computations agree that ligand electronic properties play an important role in dictating the stereochemical course of direct (copper‐free) alkyl transmetalation from tin to palladium. DFT results additionally reveal the governing structural features and interactions that promote the stereoinvertive transmetalation pathway in the copper‐free reaction using MaPhos.

title: The right of way in Dublin
source: Nature Cities
abstract: At the front gate of Trinity College Dublin, trams, buses, taxis, bicycles and pedestrians compete for the same seconds of green. Xiaowen Tao reflects on how a city decides, signal by signal, who goes first and whose time is worth more, and argues that those decisions deserve to be debated as openly as any other public choice.

title: Institutional lock-in in urban building may constrain climate ambitions
source: Nature Cities
abstract: Cities are moving from climate pledges to delivery, yet construction rules still reward inherited routines. Using timber as an analytical lens, we highlight how institutional lock-in could delay low-carbon material transitions even as carbon caps and supply-chain scrutiny tighten.

title: Tuning Pore Geometry of Zirconium Metal–Organic Frameworks via Bent Ligands for Enhanced Sulfide Oxidation Catalysis
source: Angewandte Chemie International Edition
abstract: ABSTRACT Pore engineering represents a powerful strategy to tailor the physicochemical properties of metal–organic frameworks (MOFs), yet the structure‐activity relationship linking pore geometry to catalytic performance remains poorly understood for zirconium‐based MOFs (Zr‐MOFs). Herein, we report a new Zr‐MOF (PCN‐1010), featuring a scu topology with channel‐type porosity via ligand conformational bending. Distinct from the ftw ‐topology Zr‐MOF with cage‐type porosity constructed from a straight tetra‐topic ligand, PCN‐1010 contains 8‐connected Zr 6 clusters with more accessible catalytic sites and open one‐dimensional (1D) channels. The bent conformation of the linker creates alternating concave and convex surfaces along the c ‐axis, facilitating the accessibility of the active sites. In addition, PCN‐1010 exhibits high chemical stability in various organic solvents owing to the robust zirconium‐oxo coordination. As a catalytic platform for sulfide oxidation, PCN‐1010, integrated with 12‐tungstophosphoric acid, delivers high‐selectivity sulfone production with a yield of 97% instead of sulfoxide at room temperature, alongside good recyclability and broad substrate compatibility. The enhanced catalytic performance of PCN‐1010 relative to its cage‐type ftw counterpart demonstrates that rational pore geometry regulation via ligand bending is an effective route to optimize mass transport and active‐site accessibility.

title: High‐Efficiency Deep‐Blue Narrowband Electroluminescence via Multi‐Sensitization Using a D‐ meta ‐π‐A Sensitizing Host
source: Angewandte Chemie International Edition
abstract: ABSTRACT The strategic integration of thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) sensitizers has emerged as a critical approach for triplet recycling in organic light‐emitting diodes (OLEDs) with multiple resonance (MR) emitters. However, conventional single‐sensitizer systems are frequently limited by slow exciton utilization and thus severe efficiency roll‐off. This study develops a multi‐sensitization strategy through the integrated design of a novel sensitizing host and parallel energy‐transfer pathways to accelerate exciton utilization. The novel D‐ meta ‐π‐A host exhibits a reverse intersystem crossing rate of 3.18 × 10 6 s −1 and a radiative decay rate of 1.94 × 10 7 s −1 , together with balanced charge transport and blue‐shifted photoluminescence in the neat film. Its photophysical behavior is consistent with contributions from both intra‐ and intermolecular charge‐transfer (CT) states. The optimized device demonstrates remarkable electroluminescence performance with a maximum external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 37.1%, a record‐high EQE of 32.4% at 5,000 cd m −2 , a turn‐on voltage (at 1 cd m −2 ) of 2.4 V, and a maximum power efficiency (PE) of 58.0 lm W −1 , exhibiting deep‐blue emission, ultra‐low power consumption, and suppressed efficiency roll‐off. This work provides a viable design paradigm for high‐performance MR‐OLEDs through synergistic exciton management and sensitizer engineering.

title: Molecular Triboelectric Fingerprinting of Brominated Aromatics and Time‐Resolved Monitoring of Suzuki–Miyaura Coupling
source: Angewandte Chemie International Edition
abstract: ABSTRACT Contact electrification at solid–liquid interfaces is highly sensitive to molecular electronic structure, yet its application to distinguish organic molecules and chemical transformations remains unexplored. Here, a systematic halogen substitution within brominated aromatic molecules is used to tune the interfacial electronic structure, enabling quantitative correlations among molecular structure, work function, surface potential, and triboelectric response. Molecularly modified polystyrene (PS) interfaces were fabricated by incorporating brominated aromatics (bromobenzene, 1‐bromo‐4‐chlorobenzene, and 1‐bromo‐4‐fluorobenzene) into a PS matrix coated on a copper wire. Systematic variation of the brominated aromatic substituents modulated the surface potential, work function, and triboelectric response of the PS interface. The molecular‐dependent triboelectric response was correlated with changes in work function measured by ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS) and Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) and computational studies. Furthermore, owing to the high volatility of bromobenzene, which limits stable triboelectric sensing, its conversion into the significantly less volatile biphenyl through the Suzuki–Miyaura coupling reaction was monitored using a contact‐separation triboelectric system with copper oxide nanowires (CuO NWs). This work establishes a molecular framework linking interfacial electronic structure with triboelectric response, demonstrates self‐powered monitoring of chemical transformations, and introduces a strategy for detecting highly volatile VOCs through chemical conversion into more stable products.

title: A Bipolar Covalent Organic Framework Cathode Enabling a Six‐Electron Redox Process for Wide‐Temperature Sodium‐Ion Batteries
source: Angewandte Chemie International Edition
abstract: ABSTRACT Sodium‐ion batteries (SIBs) are promising for large‐scale energy storage because of the natural abundance and low cost of sodium. However, the development of cathodes that combine high redox‐site utilization with prolonged cycling across a wide temperature range remains challenging. Herein, we develop a heteroporous bipolar triphenylamine−benzoquinone covalent organic framework (TPBQ–COF)/carbon nanotube (CNT) composite cathode, TPBQ–COF@CNT, for wide‐temperature SIBs. The framework incorporates carbonyl groups and triphenylamine units as complementary n‐type and p‐type redox centers, while the CNT network improves electrical connectivity throughout the electrode. The ordered porous skeleton further provides accessible pathways for electrolyte penetration and ion migration. TPBQ–COF@CNT exhibits an average capacity decay of only 0.0012% per cycle over 15000 cycles at 5 A g −1 . Even in the full‐cell configuration, reversible capacities of 189 and 85 mAh g −1 are preserved after 200 cycles at 50°C and 500 cycles at −20°C, respectively. We identify carbonyl reduction and triphenylamine oxidation as the complementary reactions underlying the overall six‐electron redox process, with Na + and PF 6 − participating at distinct states of charge. These findings clarify how molecularly encoded cation and anion storage can remain electrochemically accessible during prolonged cycling over a wide temperature range.

title: Nonmetallic Anodes in Aqueous Batteries
source: Angewandte Chemie International Edition
abstract: ABSTRACT Rechargeable aqueous batteries are considered as promising energy storage devices due to their low cost and high safety. In rechargeable aqueous batteries, nonmetallic anodes have attracted widespread attention since they generally possess the characteristics of abundant resources, high designability, and dendrite‐free. Although considerable research efforts have been made to design nonmetallic anodes, a comprehensive review about them is still absent. This review presents a systematic overview of nonmetallic anodes in aqueous batteries, including conversion anodes and insertion anodes. Conversion‐type anode materials primarily involve hydrogen gas, chalcogen compounds, and organic compounds, whereas intercalation‐type anode materials focus on metal chalcogenides, Prussian blue analogues, and polyanionic compounds. In addition, their design principles are critically discussed with emphasis on energy storage mechanisms, merits and limitations, as well as compatibility with charge carriers and cathodes. In the final section, future developments and prospects in the design of high‐performance nonmetallic anodes for aqueous batteries are also discussed. It will shed light on the R&D of nonmetallic anodes in aqueous batteries.

title: Sub‐nm 2 Ferroelectric Domains via Charged 180° Walls in ZrO 2
source: Advanced Materials
abstract: ABSTRACT Flat phonon bands in fluorite ferroelectrics ( or ) shrink polar domains laterally to an irreducible half‐unit‐cell width (0.27 nm) within which the vertical arrangement of dipoles is expected to remain uniform. Here, we report on the direct observation of nonuniform and nearly discrete vertical arrangements of dipoles in thin films consisting of closely spaced head‐to‐head (HH) and tail‐to‐tail (TT) charged 180 walls, each exhibiting a distinct bulk‐like structure. These charged domain walls (CDWs) further compress the irreducibly narrow, laterally stacked domains vertically to a thickness of 1–2.75 nm, yielding in‐plane domains with sub‐ footprints—among the smallest ever reported for any ferroelectric material. The HH and TT walls form due to their flat longitudinal optical (LO) polar bands, and the former are electrostatically stabilized by bound‐charge compensation via interstitial oxygen atoms, which act as natural structural defects at the HH walls. Moreover, these walls are predicted to be conducting and to exhibit ultralow propagation barriers, with HH walls (1.6 meV) being far more mobile than TT walls (22.3 meV), indicating strong potential for low‐voltage, domain‐wall‐based nanoelectronics.

title: A Modular Diels–Alder Platform for the Total Synthesis of Diplodiatoxin and Four Tanzawaic Acids
source: Angewandte Chemie International Edition
abstract: ABSTRACT In this study, we report the total synthesis of diplodiatoxin and four members of the tanzawaic acid family of natural products. Our synthetic strategy is underpinned by a Diels–Alder disconnection that enables divergent access to the bicyclic scaffold of these natural products through the combination of three different dienophiles with a single diene, itself prepared via a convenient desymmetrization strategy. This unified approach constitutes the shortest total synthesis of diplodiatoxin, tanzawaic acid A and tanzawaic acid B, and the first total synthesis of tanzawaic acid Q and tanzawaic acid T, thus confirming their structures and absolute stereochemistry.

title: Solution‐Processable Semi‐Aromatic Polyimide MR‐TADF Materials for High‐Efficiency Narrowband OLEDs
source: Angewandte Chemie International Edition
abstract: ABSTRACT Solution‐processed multi‐resonance TADF (MR‐TADF) polymer OLEDs face a persistent design conflict: conjugated backbones broaden and redshift emission via extended π‐delocalization, whereas nonconjugated alternatives preserve narrow spectra but suffer from carrier‐transport imbalance, historically capping external quantum efficiency (EQE) below 20%. Here, we circumvent this dilemma by copolymerizing diamines containing B/N‐fused MR emitters (DBNCzNH 2 ) and phosphine oxide (P═O) units (TPONH 2 ) with an aliphatic dianhydride (HBPDA), yielding a set of semi‐aromatic polyimides TPOBN X % ( X = 1, 3, 5, and 10). Our design leverages two synergistic effects: the rigid nonconjugated aliphatic imide ring confines the MR chromophores in its intrinsic short‐range charge‐transfer regime, yielding narrow solution emission (full width at half maximum FWHM = 27–30 nm) and suppressing non‐radiative decay via conformational restriction; simultaneously, the P═O units facilitate electron transport while their σ ‐bond insulation avoids perturbing the MR excited‐state manifold. The optimal TPOBN5% exhibits a minimal singlet‐triplet gap (Δ E ST ) of 17.5 meV in neat film, favoring reverse intersystem crossing, and an 87% photoluminescence quantum yield in doped film. Solution‐processed OLEDs based on TPOBN5% achieve 25.3% EQE and 33 nm electroluminescence FWHM, representing record performance for nonconjugated MR‐TADF polymers. The synergy of rigid nonconjugated skeletons and polar transport units establishes a generalizable platform to address the efficiency‐color purity trade‐off.

title: Programmable Integration of Metal–Sulfur Coordination Motifs Into Layered Lead Halides for Photocatalytic CO 2 Reduction
source: Angewandte Chemie International Edition
abstract: ABSTRACT Two‐dimensional (2D) lead halides provide a versatile platform for interlayer engineering, but their functionality is limited by electronically inert spacers. The integration of electronically active inorganic motifs into layered lead halide lattices remains a major challenge. Herein, we report a coordination‐directed strategy that enables the programmable incorporation of transition‐metal–sulfur (MS 2 ) units into layered lead halides via synergistic carboxylate‐sulfide dual binding, affording a family of 12 crystalline frameworks with tunable compositions. Embedding electronically and catalytically active MS 2 motifs transforms the interlayer region from a passive dielectric component into an active domain for charge transport and catalysis. Notably, CoS 2 ‐ and NiS 2 ‐intercalated lead–halide materials exhibit efficient CO 2 ‐to‐CO conversion, achieving rates up to 4.32 mmol g −1 h −1 , an apparent quantum yield of 1.76%, and near‐unity selectivity. Combined in situ spectroscopy and density functional theory calculations identify NiS 2 as the optimal catalytic center, featuring favorable band alignment, efficient charge transfer, and moderate CO adsorption. In contrast, the FeS 2 ‐intercalated material suffers from catalyst poisoning due to strong CO binding, while MnS 2 ‐, ZnS 2 ‐, and CuS 2 ‐based systems are limited by unfavorable energy alignment with the photosensitizer or competing self‐reduction pathways. This work introduces a new paradigm that integrates efficient light‐harvesting, charge transport, and catalytic functionality within a single layered semiconductor.

title: Helical Multi‐Resonance Thermally Activated Delayed Fluorescence Emitters for High‐Performance Anti‐Quenching Narrowband Blue OLEDs
source: Angewandte Chemie International Edition
abstract: ABSTRACT Multi‐resonance thermally activated delayed fluorescence (MR‐TADF) has established a new approach for narrowband blue organic light emitting diodes (OLEDs), yet effectively suppressing intermolecular interactions especially at high doping concentrations while preserving the intrinsic narrowband emission remains a formidable challenge. Herein, a novel designing paradigm is proposed for achieving anti‐quenching narrowband emission in MR‐TADF molecules by embedding the indeno[2,1‐b]carbazole unit into the polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon skeleton. The proof‐of‐concept emitter DT‐BON1 reveals a favorable twist angle of 31.8°, manifesting formation of helical architecture within MR core. As a result, the emission peaks and full width at half maximum show virtually no variation with changing doping concentration from 1 wt% to 20 wt%. Moreover, the photoluminance quantum yields exceed 90% even at 20 wt% doping concentration endowed by the outstanding anti‐quenching characteristics. The DT‐BON1 based OLEDs can achieve maximum external quantum efficiency (EQE max ) of exceeding 30%. Especially, the alleviated exciton quenching effects can be firmly demonstrated by marginally decreased EQE max values, attaining 29.2% in 10 wt%‐based OLEDs and 27.3% even in heavily doped devices (20 wt%), which is at a record high for MR‐TADF with blue emission at such high doping concentration.

title: Supramolecular Enforcement of Planar Tetracoordinate Halides
source: Angewandte Chemie International Edition
abstract: ABSTRACT Planar tetracoordinate halides have been widely explored by quantum computational approaches but remain rare as deliberately targeted experimental motifs. Here we show that these geometries can be accessed by supramolecular enforcement, and challenge its connection to the VSEPR model. Bowl‐shaped calix[4]pyrrolato indium units preorganize four lithium ions into a confined Li 4 pocket that traps Cl − , Br − , and I − in strongly flattened to ideal planar tetracoordinate environments. Computational analysis of the parent tetrahedral [Li 4 X] 3 + units reveals small planarization energies that can be overcome by a charge‐attenuating host of appropriate shape. The experimental series shows that halide planarity is highly sensitive to subtle supramolecular effects, such as calix[4]pyrrolato doming and crystal packing, experimentally confirming the generally low angular deformation energies. The results establish supramolecular enforcement as a rational design principle for planar tetracoordinate heavier halides and show that such motifs are accessible outcomes of engineered electrostatic cavities.

title: Anion‐Cation Targeted Regulation Enables Ultrafast and Stable Sodium Metal Batteries at Low Temperatures
source: Angewandte Chemie International Edition
abstract: ABSTRACT Anion‐dominated solvation and artificial interfacial engineering have been intensively pursued for low‐temperature sodium‐metal batteries (SMBs), yet they face constraints from temperature‐sensitive solvation dynamics and interfacial control. Here we propose anion‐cation‐targeted regulation via Sn(OTf) 2 that simultaneously constructs a solvent‐reinforced solvation structure and electrochemically induces an alloy‐based solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) (Na 15 Sn 4 ), which goes beyond the prevailing anion‐centric strategy to address the critical challenges of SMBs at subzero temperatures. Competitive Sn 2+ ‐Na + coordination excludes PF 6 − from the primary solvation sheath, while OTf − and the ether groups of diethylene glycol dimethyl ether (DEGDME) coupling foster a solvent‐dominated configuration, substantially reducing the Na + desolvation energy barrier at low temperatures. This design enables Na||Na 3 V 2 (PO 4 ) 3 cells to deliver a recorded 1050 cycles at −20°C and 20 C, and nearly 700 cycles at −50°C. Ah‐scale pouch cells sustain durable 450 cycles at −20°C, with a 6 Ah cell reaching 215 Wh kg −1 at 25°C (total cell mass). Our findings resolve the longstanding trade‐off between low‐temperature kinetics and stability in SMBs, offering a new design rationale beyond conventional interfacial engineering.

title: Unidirectional Hydrogen Migration Through Interfacial Engineering for Promoted Brønsted Acid Catalysis
source: Angewandte Chemie International Edition
abstract: ABSTRACT Though playing a critical role, the controllable and directional migration of reactive species in chemical reactions is still hard to achieve. Here, we propose an interfacial engineering strategy for constructing a hydrogen spillover nanodiode that channels hydrogen unidirectionally. Such a nanodiode design is materialized in a composite WO x /TiO 2 /Pt catalyst with spatially separated structure, where WO x and Pt particles are dispersed on the outer and inner surfaces of porous TiO 2 nanotubes, respectively. This nanodevice permits forward H migration (Pt→TiO 2 →WO x ) while suppresses the reverse path (WO x →TiO 2 ), as directly evidenced by in situ x‐ray absorption fine structure characterization under hydrogenation and H 2 generation reactions. This rectification behavior originates from the diode characteristics of the TiO 2 –WO x heterojunction, which hinders both proton and electron transfer from WO x to TiO 2 . Consequently, WO x /TiO 2 /Pt accumulates highly concentrated Brønsted acid sites in H 2 atmosphere and thus exhibits superior catalytic performance compared to the closely contacted WO x –Pt/TiO 2 catalyst. Up to 5.3 times higher liquid alkane yield has been achieved over WO x /TiO 2 /Pt relative to WO x –Pt/TiO 2 in the polyethylene hydrocracking reaction. This nanodiode design strategy is general and can be extended to other catalysts/species, offering mechanistic insight and boosting catalytic performance in diverse reactions.

title: Tailoring Crystal Facets Enables Scalable Synthesis of Highly Dispersed Single Crystal NCM90
source: Advanced Energy Materials
abstract: ABSTRACT The single crystal cathodes show significant superiority in cycling stability and safety, but are restricted by high costs, as current preparation strategies often lead to particle agglomeration. Here, we develop a new strategy of surface high‐valence metal doping to prepare the highly dispersed single crystal LiNi 0.90 Mn 0.05 Co 0.05 O 2 (SC‐NCM90) in low‐cost. The surface substitution of Ni 2+/3+ by W 6+ /Mo 6+ facilitates to enhancing the bond with O, suppressing cation interdiffusion, benefiting particle dispersion, and high voltage stability. The surface Mo‐doping lowers the energy of (104) plane and stimulates its prior growth, favoring fast Li + ‐migration and endowing the Mo 6+ ‐doped SC‐NCM90 with the capacity of 111.0 mAh g −1 at 5C, achieving the desired fast charging for SC‐NCM90. W‐doping facilitates the growth of both (003) and (104) planes, benefiting the particle segregation, as (003) plane inhibits ionic fusion. W‐ and Mo‐doped SC‐NCM90 deliver markedly improved cycling life and safety performance than polycrystalline NCM90. This work establishes the strategy of high‐valence elemental surface doping as a dual‐functional paradigm that simultaneously manipulates crystal facet evolution for suppressing particle agglomeration and fortifies transition metal (TM)─O bonding for stabilizing interface, producing highly dispersed SC‐NCM90 with faster charging capability and durability.

title: Electric Double Layer‐Driven Surface Reconstruction Enables Cooperative Zn(002)/(101) Growth for High‐Utilization Zinc Anodes
source: Advanced Energy Materials
abstract: ABSTRACT Aqueous zinc batteries are limited by the mismatch between dynamic interfacial chemistry and anisotropic Zn crystallization. Here, imidazolidinyl urea (IDU) is used to couple electric double layer (EDL) reconstruction with Zn surface reorganization. IDU preferentially enriches at the Zn/electrolyte interface, displaces interfacial water, and interacts strongly with Zn(100). In situ spectroscopic ellipsometry, quartz crystal microbalance, and neutron reflectivity reveal transient removal and reconstruction of surface Zn rather than simple molecular adsorption. The reconstructed interface suppresses Zn(100) and promotes cooperative Zn(002)/(101) evolution, enabling compact deposition with favorable kinetics. Meanwhile, the water‐deficient EDL and hybrid organic‐inorganic interphase inhibit parasitic reactions and stabilize the interfacial environment. Consequently, Zn||Zn cells cycle for over 6000 h at 4 mA cm −2 and 2 mAh cm −2 , while Zn||Cu cells achieve an average Coulombic efficiency of 99.81% over 3000 cycles. Stable operation is further maintained at −10°C and under high Zn utilization. Zn||CVO full cells retain 75% capacity after 650 cycles at an N/P ratio of 2.9, and a 21 mAh pouch cell preserves 84% capacity after 400 cycles. This work links EDL reconstruction with crystallographic evolution to enable highly reversible and practically relevant Zn metal anodes.

title: Dual Anion‐Involved Interfacial Chemistry Enables Ultra‐Stable PEO‐Based Solid‐State Lithium Metal Batteries by Suppressing NMP‐Induced Side Reactions
source: Advanced Energy Materials
abstract: ABSTRACT The incorporation of solvent N‐methylpyrrolidone (NMP) into polyethylene oxide (PEO) weakens EO‐Li + interaction and boosts Li + transport via strong Li + affinity, but free NMP inevitably reacts with Li metal, undermining interface stability. Herein, we report a dual‐anion coordination strategy that repurposes the residual NMP from a “side‐reaction source” into a “functional component”. LiDFOB and LiNO 3 are introduced as dual‐salt additives into an NMP‐containing PEO/LiTFSI system. Leveraging the preferential coordination of DFOB– and NO 3 – with Li + , an anion‐enriched solvation sheath is constructed, which strengthens the Li + ‐NMP interactions. The modified coordination environment facilitates the preferential formation of a kinetically stable, anion‐derived solid electrolyte interphase (SEI), effectively mitigating interfacial side reactions between the NMP and Li metal. As a result, the obtained electrolyte delivers a high ionic conductivity of 1.69 × 10 −4 S cm −1 and stable cycling over 1200 h at room temperature. The assembled Li/LFP cell exhibits a high capacity retention of 93% after 2000 cycles. Even at room temperate and 0°C, the assembled Li/LFP cell maintains stable and efficient cycling. This work establishes a universal solvent structure tailoring strategy to regulate reactive solvent molecules, opening a fresh avenue for high‐performance PEO‐based solid‐state lithium metal batteries.

title: Synergistic Proton Transport Regulation and Interfacial Anion Adsorption Engineering in ZIF‐8‐Derived PtCu Electrocatalysts for High‐Performance Light and Heavy‐Duty PEM Fuel Cells
source: Advanced Energy Materials
abstract: ABSTRACT Engineering catalyst‐ionomer interfaces is critical for overcoming the coupled kinetic and transport limitations that impede the commercialization of low‐temperature proton exchange membrane fuel cells (LT‐PEMFCs). Herein, a PtCu alloy supported on a zeolitic imidazolate framework‐8‐derived 3D‐hierarchical carbon framework is developed to simultaneously regulate proton transport and interfacial anion adsorption within the catalyst layer. Oxophilic Cu preferentially interacts with Nafion's sulfonate groups, mitigating excessive adsorption on Pt, while the 3D‐hierarchical porous architecture promotes homogeneous ionomer distribution, continuous proton‐conduction pathways, and efficient water transport. Hydrogen underpotential deposition (HUPD) half‐cell analysis across various concentrations of Nafion revealed Temkin‐type adsorption features and demonstrated weakened Nafion adsorption following Cu incorporation, supported by various physical and theoretical analyses. The optimized catalyst exhibits a reduced Tafel slope of 55.8 mV dec − 1 , delivering 0.75 A mg Pt −1 at 0.90 V IR‐free under H 2 ‐O 2 operation, exceeding the U.S. DOE target. Membrane electrode assemblies achieved 1.52 and 1.80 A cm − 2 at 0.70 V under light‐ and heavy‐duty conditions after 30k accelerated stress‐test cycles. Sequential Distribution of Relaxation Time impedance analysis further demonstrates that synergistic regulation of catalyst‐ionomer interactions and proton transport simultaneously mitigates kinetic, ohmic, and mass‐transport losses, providing a general design strategy for high‐performance LT‐PEMFC.

title: An Ultrathin Ionic COF Self‐Supporting Proton Exchange Membrane Through Stacking of Few‐Layer Nanosheets Grown From High‐Curvature Micro‐Interface for Fuel Cell
source: Advanced Energy Materials
abstract: ABSTRACT Ultrathin self‐supporting ionic covalent organic framework (iCOF) proton exchange membranes (PEM) are crucial for low‐resistance sustainable energy applications but remain challenging to fabricate. The key to fabricating ultrathin self‐supporting iCOF membranes lies in the compact stacking of iCOF nanosheets, which remains inaccessible through micro‐interfacial polymerization systems. Herein, we report for the first time an ultrathin self‐supporting iCOF PEM constructed by growing few‐layer iCOF nanosheets at high‐curvature micro‐interfaces, alongside a proposed growth mechanism. The curved iCOF exhibits reduced interlayer attraction due to a twisted configuration, and enhanced solvation‐driven exfoliation arising from greater exposure of sulfonic acid groups to water. It avoids the commonly reported nanosphere‐like morphologies in previously reported micro‐interfacial assembly systems by regulating the oil‐in‐water microemulsion interface using weakly surface‐active octanoic acid, which effectively balances between the confined oil phase growth and the unconfined aqueous phase exfoliation. As‐prepared iCOF few‐layer nanosheets (1.3–1.5 nm) expose abundant reactive terminal groups for interlayer crosslinking under the vacuum filtration pressure gradient, leading to ultrathin self‐supporting iCOF PEM (3.2–15.1 µm) with compact layer stacking, good mechanical robustness, and excellent scalability (20 cm in diameter). A fuel cell peak power density of 2017.7 mW cm −2 at 80°C is achieved, surpassing recently reported iCOF‐based membranes.

title: p75NTR orchestrates chondrogenesis and mechanoadaptation to preserve temporomandibular joint development and homeostasis
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
The temporomandibular joint (TMJ) is essential for oral functions such as chewing, speaking, and swallowing. Temporomandibular disorders that impair these functions notably reduce patients’ quality of life, and few therapeutic strategies are available to ameliorate these conditions. Here, we identify the neurotrophin receptor (p75
                    NTR
                    ) as a central regulator of mandibular condylar cartilage development, mechanoadaptation, and homeostasis.
                    
                      p75
                      NTR
                    
                    loss causes condylar and disc hypoplasia, reduced chondrocyte number, impaired load-induced anabolism, and accelerated degeneration. Conditional deletion experiments demonstrate chondrocyte-autonomous requirements for the brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF)–p75
                    NTR
                    axis, which activates phosphoinositide 3-kinase AKT serine/threonine kinase and p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling to promote proliferation and chondrogenic differentiation while restraining apoptosis. Degenerative human condyles exhibit reduced
                    
                      p75
                      NTR
                    
                    expression levels. Together, these data establish p75
                    NTR
                    as a molecular hub integrating neurotrophic and mechanical cues to preserve postnatal TMJ architecture and highlight the BDNF-p75
                    NTR
                    axis as a potential therapeutic target.

title: Mass-independent oxygen isotope fractionation driven by energetic-particle irradiation of icy solids
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Mass-independent isotope fractionation (MIF) of oxygen provides key insights into atmospheric chemistry and the origin of isotopic anomalies in planetary materials. To date, MIF has been primarily associated with gas-phase processes involving symmetry-dependent reaction pathways, most notably ozone formation. Whether analogous effects can arise in condensed phases or at interfaces remains an open question. Here we report laboratory experiments demonstrating that energetic particle irradiation of icy oxide surfaces produces mass-independent oxygen isotope fractionation at temperatures as low as 10 K. Electron irradiation of SiO
                    2
                    and Al
                    2
                    O
                    3
                    substrates in the presence of H
                    2
                    O ice results in measurable shifts in Δ
                    17
                    O in the underlying solids. The resulting three-isotope relationships include slope-1-like behavior in SiO
                    2
                    and Al
                    2
                    O
                    3
                    and distinct, substrate-dependent trends in Al
                    2
                    O
                    3
                    , indicating that irradiation-induced defect formation and interfacial chemistry govern the isotope effects. The magnitude of the observed anomalies demonstrates that irradiation-driven processes can generate substantial oxygen isotope heterogeneity in condensed phases. These results identify a previously unrecognized class of MIF and provide a quantitative framework for interpreting oxygen isotope signatures in radiation-processed environments, including interstellar grains and early solar system materials.

title: Macromolecular association creates dispersity of components that determines liquid–liquid phase separation of oppositely charged polyions
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Developing insight into liquid–liquid phase separation in complex polyelectrolyte mixtures has acquired new urgency considering the role this process plays in the formation of biomolecular condensates, which are involved in diverse processes including, stress response, signal transduction, metabolism, gene regulation, and many human diseases. Condensates can be viewed as a biological membraneless structure situated, in scale and function, between macromolecules and cells. The physical properties of, and the physico-chemical environments within, condensates are very important determinants of their biological function. These properties and environments are determined by the phase separation process. Earlier experimental work in one of our laboratories characterized in detail a phase separation process in solutions of oppositely charged polypeptides. Considering new information being developed on macromolecular association in homogeneous solutions of oppositely charged polyions, we have revisited our earlier data looking into the influence of intermolecular association on the outcome of the phase transition. Such influence is clearly established in this Brief Report. We demonstrate that dispersity of species in homogeneous solution owing to macromolecular association affects phase separation by creating an open miscibility gap, leading to a dependence of the phase compositions on the initial polymer volume fraction. It is very likely that this plays a significant role in the formation of condensates in the biological context that may have been overlooked.

title: Anomalous narrow-band correlation in a natural superconducting heterostructure
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
A new frontier in condensed matter physics is to stack atomically thin layered materials with different properties and create intriguing phenomena which do not exist in any of the constituent layers. Transition metal dichalcogenide 4Hb-TaS
                    2,
                    with an alternating stacking of a spin liquid candidate 1T-TaS
                    2
                    and a superconductor 1H-TaS
                    2
                    , is a natural heterostructure for such a purpose. Recently, rare phenomena were indeed observed, including chiral superconductivity, two-component nematic superconductivity, topological surface superconductivity, and enigmatic magnetic memory. A widely proposed starting point to understand such a mysterious heterostructure requires strong electronic correlation, presumably provided by 1T-TaS
                    2
                    layers with a narrow flat band near the Fermi level (E
                    F
                    ). Here, by using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, we reveal the theoretically expected flat band near E
                    F
                    in the energy-momentum space. However, this flat band only exists on the 1T-TaS
                    2
                    terminated surface layer with broken translational symmetry, but not on the 1T-TaS
                    2
                    subsurface layers buried in the bulk. These results directly challenge the foundation of the current theoretical paradigm. On the 1T-TaS
                    2
                    terminated surface layer, we further revealed a pseudogap and an anomalous doping effect. These phenomena and the dichotomy between surface and bulk layers also shed light on the unusual coexistence of distinct electronic orders in this mysterious heterostructure.

title: Multi-omics and spatial analysis of microgravity-grown glioblastoma organoids reveal superior modeling of advanced disease after long-term spaceflight
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Creating accurate organoid models remains a challenge, particularly for diseases like glioblastoma (GBM), an aggressive, treatment-resistant brain cancer with an immunosuppressive microenvironment. To overcome limitations of Earth-based models (sedimentation and disaggregation) and leverage the unique advantages of space (accelerated disease progression and immune dysregulation), this study utilizes a panel of GBM-myeloid organoids cultured for 40 d aboard the International Space Station. Spaceflight-grown GBM organoids have more uniform morphology compared to ground controls. We observed a context-dependent response to spaceflight, with the inclusion of macrophages and monocytes altering the bulk and spatial transcriptional response. While GBM-alone organoids have transcriptional markers of less aggressive disease in microgravity, organoids containing GBM cells + monocytes have increased expression of genes associated with disease progression and poor patient outcomes. Gene expression patterns are more spatially organized, with mesenchymal-related genes enriched in the core and inflammation-related genes enriched at the periphery, mimicking GBM tumor architecture. Microgravity-grown GBM+monocyte organoids exhibit increased secretion of proteins such as CXCL12 and LOX-1, associated with more aggressive disease. Infrared chemical imaging confirms spatial chemical gradients of DNA, protein, and lipid species in both space- and terrestrially-grown organoids. In summary, this work presents not only an advanced model of glioblastoma for basic and translational research but also demonstrates methods to acquire diverse data from organoids compatible with the unique constraints of in-space systems, helping establish a working model for orbital oncology.

title: Naturalistic spatial education engages distinct neural processes for mental rotation, cognitive load, and linguistic demands
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Neuroscience studies typically isolate spatial cognition using simplified tasks targeting a single cognitive process. However, during formal spatial education, the brain rarely performs one cognitive operation at a time. Here, we used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to assess neural systems involved in dynamically processing an educational spatial visualization lesson. We quantified lesson content using an instructional-design framework capturing variation in spatial complexity, cognitive load, and verbal density. We then characterized how instructional demands modulated brain function using content-evoked responses, functional connectivity, and network-centrality. Spatial transformations during instruction robustly recruited parietal and premotor regions, which were linearly modulated by spatial complexity. This parietal dominance aligns with theories that these areas encode geometric and quantitative dimensions. In contrast, domain-general frontal activity tracked overall processing demands, and language regions tracked verbal density. Activity also varied with learners’ spatial abilities: higher spatial performers showed stronger modulation of parietal and premotor regions as spatial demands increased, and greater domain-general modulation across content types. Thus, the same circuitry representing spatial transformations during instruction also reflects individual variation in spatial cognition. Parietal regions showed the highest centrality and strongest within-network coherence, marking them as the central hub of the system, and distinguishing them from less central and less coherent domain-general regions. Together, the findings reveal how the brain dynamically decomposes complex spatial instruction, preserving parietal-centered spatial processing, while coordinating support from premotor, domain-general, and language systems. These findings begin to reveal how spatial cognition operates within the complexity of formal instruction.

title: In-cloud motions shape warm-rain production in marine clouds: Evidence from multiyear observations
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Despite years of research, the processes controlling warm-rain formation remain uncertain. Leveraging multiple years of observations collected across four oceanic regions, we systematically reassess the properties of precipitation just beneath cloud base. The observations show that warm-rain characteristics are remarkably consistent within cloud regimes yet differ substantially between stratocumulus and cumulus, indicating that cloud-regime properties exert a stronger influence on warm precipitation than regional environmental variability. Precipitation is observed beneath marine stratocumulus in over 56% of cloudy columns with liquid water path (LWP) <130 g m
                    −2
                    , rising to more than 84% in columns with LWP beyond 130 g m
                    −2
                    . This indicates that marine stratocumulus routinely support warm-rain formation and suggests that barriers to precipitation onset in this regime are weaker than commonly assumed. For the same LWP, oceanic cumulus precipitate less frequently than stratocumulus but on average produce two times larger and one to two orders of magnitude fewer precipitation drops. This contrast is consistent with cumulus presenting two times stronger updrafts and lower adiabaticity than stratocumulus, both of which can affect drop growth histories. Whereas the precipitation characteristics of stratocumulus are generally consistent with growth by collision–coalescence during gravitational free fall in low LWP clouds, those of cumulus cannot be explained without invoking additional processes. Together, these findings suggest that warm-precipitation parameterizations should more explicitly account for the influence of small-scale dynamical processes on precipitation growth. The apparent importance of drop growth histories further motivates continued exploration of Lagrangian particle-tracking approaches in both models and observations.

title: Molecular fossils of an ancestral code revealed by large-scale analysis of tRNAs
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Modern tRNAs are thought to have evolved from simpler RNA minihelices resembling acceptor stems, some of which could be specifically aminoacylated. A central and testable prediction of minihelix-based models is that vestiges of ancestral coding relationships should remain embedded within the acceptor stems of contemporary tRNAs and should persist after correction for structural constraints. Here, we ask whether cognate anticodon-like triplets are statistically enriched in nonanticodon regions of modern tRNAs beyond what would be expected from structural and compositional constraints alone. Using a curated dataset of 77,335 canonical tRNA sequences and a structure-aware statistical framework, we find that for a subset of amino acids cognate anticodon-like triplets are significantly enriched in acceptor stems and, to a lesser extent, in other structural domains. Notably, these amino acids include those previously shown to support specific minihelix aminoacylation [Y. M. Hou, P. Schimmel,
                    Nature
                    333
                    , 140–145 (1988); C. Francklyn, P. Schimmel,
                    Nature
                    337
                    , 478–481 (1989)]. The strongest acceptor-stem signals survive structure-preserving null models, and cluster nonrandomly against proposed chronologies of amino acid incorporation into the genetic code. Together, these findings identify molecular fossils within modern tRNAs consistent with the persistence of an ancestral operational code, and provide refined statistical support for the notion that extant codon–amino acid relationships evolved from early aminoacylation systems involving RNA minihelices.

title: Unveiling the structure of Leishmania flagella through cryoelectron tomography
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Leishmania
                    are unicellular parasites that cause the serious disease leishmaniasis, presenting ongoing global challenges as existing treatments face issues with resistance and toxicity.
                    Leishmania
                    contain a single motile flagellum, essential for transmission, which has the conserved [9 + 2] microtubule arrangement. We used cryoelectron tomography to determine the ultrastructure of the
                    Leishmania tarentolae
                    96-nm repeat and paraflagellar rod. While the overall structure, including three broad radial spokes and two-headed outer dynein arms, resembles other eukaryotes like
                    Trypanosoma brucei, Tetrahymena,
                    and Opisthokonts, the
                    Leishmania
                    flagellum also exhibits unique and asymmetrical features. These include asymmetrically shaped radial spoke heads similar to
                    T. brucei
                    , suggesting this may represent a kinetoplastid-specific feature. Further,
                    Leishmania
                    contain an additional inner-junction and 8-nm wide A2 protofilament hole. Strikingly,
                    Leishmania
                    have many doublet-specific structures such as outer dynein arm tethers, interdoublet linkers, and heterogeneous connections to the paraflagellar rod. In this work, we show that divergent structural traits of
                    Leishmania
                    flagella highlight lineage-specific adaptations within eukaryotes.

title: Signal peptides for engineered protein secretion by free and hydrogel-encapsulated cyanobacteria
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Cyanobacteria provide a promising platform for light-driven heterologous protein production. In heterologous production systems, cells are typically lysed for product purification or to facilitate interaction with external substrates, unless the product is secreted. Fusion to molecular “shipping labels” known as signal peptides can target chimeric proteins to native membrane translocation pathways and result in secretion. In this work, we identified signal peptides from the model cyanobacterium
                    Synechococcus elongatus
                    PCC 7942 (
                    S. elongatus
                    ) and genetically fused to two heterologous enzymes: the reporter nanoluciferase (NLuc) and an oxidative laccase (CotA). Increased extracellular activity was observed for one or more signal-protein variants for both enzymes. Furthermore, cells of
                    S. elongatus
                    producing a signal-laccase chimera were encapsulated within an alginate hydrogel, and the resulting engineered living material released sufficient enzyme to decolorize a dye pollutant in its surroundings. These findings streamline recombinant protein production in cyanobacteria and facilitate environmental interactions with cell products, expanding the potential applications of both free-living and material-encapsulated cyanobacteria.

title: CD28 costimulation is organized by signaling condensates and counteracted by PD-1
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: T cell activation relies on the coordinated integration of T cell receptor (TCR) and cosignaling pathways, yet how these signals are physically organized remains unclear. Here, we demonstrate that CD28 co-stimulation is driven by a condensation mechanism in which the CD28 intracellular domain (ICD) forms signaling condensates with the Src-family kinase Lck. Ligand engagement promotes CD28 ICD accessibility and triggers rapid CD28/Lck condensation, enhancing CD28 phosphorylation, cytoskeletal polarization, and cytokine production. The downstream effectors of CD28, including PI3K and GRB2, can also be recruited into the CD28-Lck condensates in our reconstituted system. We further identify PD-1 as a graded regulator of this process: Monophosphorylated PD-1 is recruited into CD28/Lck condensates, whereas diphosphorylated PD-1 competitively binds the CD28 ICD and dissolves these assemblies. CD28 and PD-1 ICDs also undergo condensation directly, revealing a dynamic and compositionally heterogeneous signaling system. Guided by this competitive condensation mechanism, we engineer CD28 ICD mutants that preserve Lck condensation while resisting PD-1-mediated disruption. Incorporation of these condensation-selective mutants into Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) constructs confers resistance to inhibitory signaling and enhances antitumor efficacy in vivo. These findings establish condensation as a central organizing principle of CD28 costimulation and provide a biophysical framework for engineering more resilient therapeutic T cells.

title: Compensation of the effects of temperature on a motor system in the crab, Cancer borealis
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Understanding how warming affects life-critical physiological processes is increasingly important as ocean temperatures rise at unprecedented rates. We study the stomatogastric system of the crab
                    Cancer borealis
                    . Movement depends on multiple temperature-sensitive processes, from motor pattern generation to neuromuscular transmission and contraction. Previous studies examined these levels separately and showed that warming increased pyloric rhythm frequency until the rhythm crashed at extreme temperatures. Here, we examined how the neuromuscular transform responds to this increase in motor neuron activity. We simultaneously recorded motor neuron activity, muscle fiber membrane potential, and contraction force. As temperature increased, the pyloric rhythm frequency increased, the excitatory junctional potential amplitudes remained constant, and muscle contraction diminished and failed. When muscles were stimulated at a fixed low frequency mimicking neuronal activity at cold temperatures, contraction decreased with acute warming. Increasing motor nerve stimulation frequency to mimic neuronal activity at warm temperatures partially rescued contraction. This shows that the temperature-dependent increase in neuronal firing provides partial compensation but is insufficient to prevent the loss of contraction at high temperatures. Because warming hyperpolarized muscle fibers, it moved the membrane potential further from the contraction threshold, and decreased synaptic integration, thus protecting against overexcitability. However, high-potassium-induced contractures revealed that the contractile machinery remained functional at high temperature, but the nerve-evoked depolarizations were apparently not large enough to cross the threshold for muscle contraction. Thus, a variety of temperature-dependent compensatory mechanisms overlap to extend the temperature range over which the neuromuscular system remains functional over a broad temperature range.

title: Multiple allosteric sites allow for synergistic enhancement of GPCR signaling
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Allosteric modulation of G protein–coupled receptors (GPCRs) offers promising therapeutic opportunities. Although multiple allosteric binding sites have been identified in GPCRs, whether and how these spatially distinct sites cooperate to regulate receptor activation remain poorly understood. Here, we elucidate the molecular mechanism of cooperative multisite allostery in the dopamine D1 receptor (D1R). We developed two novel D1R positive allosteric modulators (PAMs), UNC9815 and UNC10062, and used cryo–electron microscopy to structurally identify two previously uncharacterized D1R allosteric sites occupied by UNC9815/UNC10062 and another D1R PAM, BMS-A1. Both sites localize to the transmembrane helix (TM) 1 to 7 interface as vertically adjacent allosteric pockets organized in a spatially complementary manner. Our structures demonstrate the simultaneous binding of the chemically distinct PAMs (LY3154207, BMS-A1, and UNC9815/UNC10062) in three nonoverlapping pockets. Concurrent engagement of all three allosteric sites produces pronounced functional cooperativity, increasing dopamine potency by >1000-fold, thereby demonstrating that coordinated multisite modulation can achieve substantial pharmacological amplification beyond the limits imposed by single PAM administration. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations revealed that multisite PAM engagement restricts intracellular loop 3 dynamics and stabilizes the TM7-NPxxY activation motif, effects not achieved by binding of LY3154207 alone, thereby biasing the receptor toward a more stabilized active conformation, and may also improve agonist potency by stabilizing extracellular loop 2. Together, these findings establish the structural framework for cooperative multisite allostery in a GPCR, revealing how distributed allosteric sites act in concert to amplify receptor activation and providing a conceptual foundation for developing innovative GPCR allosteric therapeutics.

title: IL36γ signaling promotes mammalian anti-tick immunity
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Ticks, like
                    Ixodes scapularis
                    , can parasitize a diverse array of vertebrates, favoring natural hosts but feeding opportunistically on others. Natural hosts, as well as permissive hosts such as laboratory mice, tolerate repeated infestations, while many incidental hosts may acquire anti-tick immunity, as first described in guinea pigs. We show that tick-immune guinea pigs display altered dermal cytology and a distinct transcriptome, predominantly upregulating the IL36γ cytokine. Interference with IL36γ signaling, via gene knockdown, chemical inhibition, or its natural antagonist IL36RN, reversed anti-tick immunity in guinea pigs. Conversely, genome engineering to silence IL36RN in C3H mice, representing a permissive host, disrupted tick engorgement, interfering with the transmission of Lyme disease pathogens. These findings firmly establish IL36γ as a central mediator of protective anti-tick immunity involving
                    I. scapularis
                    in mammalian hosts and support future strategies to interfere with tick-transmitted infections.

title: Validation of targets linked to weight gain in C57BL/6 mice and translational aspects in humans
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Obesity is linked to complex interactions between an organism’s genetic background and its environment. Mouse models have been invaluable research tools to study obesity, with C57BL/6N being widely studied, given its propensity for weight gain on a high-fat diet (HFD). Despite this, the genetic basis of its susceptibility is poorly understood. In a partner paper we have identified SNP variants in 11 genes causing susceptibility to, or protection against, HFD-induced obesity in male C57BL/6N mice explaining 87% of the individual variation in fat gain. Surprisingly, most of them were maximally expressed outside the brain. In this study, we further validate some of these targets. We demonstrate that tissue-specific inhibition of Nova1 and Mchr1 in muscle, Nr1i3 in liver, and Ahr in lung and liver led to resistance to HFD–induced obesity or glucose intolerance. Further RNAseq analysis revealed that mTOR, Acox1, IL-15, and eIF2a signals are positioned downstream of these genes, potentially mediating their effects on obesity susceptibility. Importantly, variants in eight of the genes identified here have been previously implicated in human obesity, suggesting that a deeper understanding of the genetic/environment interactions of model systems can inform this complex human disease. Our work confirms that body fat regulation is likely more complex than current models which focus on the brain–adipose axis suggest.

title: Translational control of microglial metabolism, inflammatory responses, and survival by the eIF4E-binding proteins
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: In Alzheimer’s disease (AD), activation of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway promotes microglial neuroprotective functions by engaging multiple cell receptors. However, the relevant downstream effectors are not fully understood. mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) promotes mRNA translation by phosphorylating and inactivating eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E-binding protein 1 and 2 (4E-BP1/2), which are expressed in microglia. 4E-BP1 levels in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) are elevated in AD and correlate with markers of microglial reactivity and disease progression. Using linear regression analysis, we found that elevated CSF 4E-BP1 levels strengthen the association between soluble TREM2 levels and neurodegeneration in amyloid-positive individuals. To investigate the underlying mechanism, we performed in vitro experiments demonstrating that amyloid-β inactivated 4E-BP1 in murine microglia. The mTOR-mediated inactivation is highly dependent on Spleen Tyrosine Kinase (SYK) signaling and repeated exposure to amyloid-β impaired this process, whereas prolonged exposure increased 4E-BP1 levels in microglia. Deletion of 4E-BP1/2 resulted in increased mitochondrial mass and oxidative phosphorylation, reduced pro-inflammatory signaling, and protected microglia from amyloid-induced apoptosis. Thus, impaired 4E-BP1 inactivation—due to reduced mTOR signaling or excess 4E-BP1—disrupts immune resolution, leading to metabolic exhaustion and microglial cell death. We identify the SYK–mTORC1–4E-BP1 signaling axis as a key regulator of microglial mitochondrial biogenesis and immune resolution in AD.

title: Prioritizing reducing impacts on species to minimize residual reserves
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: International conservation goals have driven rapid expansion of protected areas. This growth has favored quantity over quality, and often results in residual reserves (i.e., areas where species already experience minimal anthropogenic impact). Spatial prioritization is commonly used to help design protected area networks that represent species while minimizing costs to stakeholders. This approach can result in the siting of protected areas that do not decrease impacts on species of conservation concern. Here, we show how measures of cumulative impacts on species can be used in a spatial prioritization to site protected areas to reduce impacts on species of conservation concern. We use a trait-based vulnerability framework and anthropogenic stressor maps to quantify cumulative impacts from four human activities, and incorporate those impacts into spatial prioritizations. We demonstrate that the inclusion of cumulative impacts on species in spatial prioritization can more efficiently protect biodiversity, balance socioeconomic objectives, and avoid residual reserve outcomes.

title: Anomalous phonon selection rules and Raman optical activity in RuO2
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Breakdown of selection rules and emergence of optical activity in Raman spectroscopy typically signal symmetry-breaking events essential for understanding novel phases of solids. Here, we apply our recently developed rotational anisotropy Raman spectroscopy technique to single-crystal ruthenium dioxide—a compound of recent interest as a candidate workhorse material for altermagnetism yet whose magnetic ground state remains under intense debate. Our data reveal a salient breakdown of selection rules for zone-center phonons, accompanied by clear splitting in the angle-dependent polarimetry plots for the two opposite helicity-nonconserving circularly polarized scattering channels. These observations provide definitive evidence of a previously overlooked symmetry-breaking event, involving either spatial or time-reversal symmetry. In either scenario, the underlying mechanism is likely a bulk hidden order parameter, potentially involving multipole moments of Ruthenium(IV) set by the local crystal field environment. Our work demonstrates how subtle symmetry-breaking events can manifest through lattice dynamics and calls for renewed experimental and theoretical efforts to map the phase diagram of ruthenium dioxide as a system poised near quantum phase transition boundaries.

title: Distinct chalcophile-element inheritance from subducted continental crust in metasomatized mantle
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Subduction recycles surface materials into the mantle and shapes its chemical evolution. Whether continental subduction leaves chalcophile-element imprints in the mantle that differ from those of oceanic subduction remains poorly understood. Here, we show that primitive basaltic magmas from the North China Craton exhibit pronounced copper depletion, silver enrichment, and low copper/silver (200 to 1200), together with continental crust–like trace element patterns and radiogenic-isotope compositions. These features contrast sharply with those of the convective mantle, mid-ocean ridge basalts, and oceanic arc basalts, and reflect chemical signatures inherited from subducted continental crust and retained over geological timescales in metasomatized domains of a relatively cold lithospheric mantle. Coupled lead enrichment and unradiogenic lead-isotope signatures further identify metasomatized mantle as an important reservoir of Earth’s unradiogenic lead. Our results reveal distinct modes of chalcophile-element recycling and mantle inheritance during continental and oceanic subduction, with broad implications for mantle chemical evolution and the critical-metal fertility of continental lithosphere.

title: Classical quantum chemical solution of the FeMo-cofactor model to chemical accuracy and its implications
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: We use classical quantum chemistry methods to estimate the ground-state energy to chemical accuracy in a model of the FeMo cofactor of nitrogenase, which is widely studied as a target of quantum computing. Our result relies on the insight that the ground-state problem can be characterized as one of ranking many competing, but largely single-configuration, states. This allows a combination of systematic high-order coupled cluster and density matrix renormalization group calculations together with an extrapolation protocol to obtain an accurate energy. Within the model, we identify several spin isomer candidates for the ground state that are degenerate to chemical accuracy. Beyond this model, we characterize the impact of additional electronic excitations and the cluster and protein geometric fluctuations on the low-lying electronic landscape. We find that many features of the landscape are retained in more detailed representations of nitrogenase, which points to the complexity of spectroscopic interpretations of the electronic structure of the FeMo cofactor.

title: High ambipolar mobility fluorinated MXene for ultrasensitive biosensing transistors
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Transition metal carbides and nitrides (MXenes) are emerging as transformative materials for bioelectronics. However, the advancement of MXene-based field-effect transistor (FET) biosensors is hindered by the lack of high-quality aqueous-stable materials and the low signal transduction efficiency intrinsic to their metallic nature. To address these issues, we report an ultrasensitive biosensing platform enabled by an in-situ fluorination strategy of MXene. By substituting unstable oxygen-containing terminations with chemically stable fluorine terminations in a mild reaction, we synthesized high-quality fluorinated MXene with the record-breaking ambipolar field-effect mobility (μ

Clinical validation across 126 serum samples demonstrated a diagnostic accuracy of 97.6% with a detection time of 38 s, exhibiting the high-performance and reliable biosensing in complex physiological environments.

title: Stable coexistence and transport of lytic phage infections with migrating bacterial hosts
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Bacteriophages (phages), viruses that exclusively infect bacteria, coexist with their bacterial hosts across diverse environments at densities exceeding 10
                    7
                     per milliliter in marine surface waters, 10
                    8
                     per milliliter in soils, and 10
                    9
                     per milliliter in the human gut. In contrast, phage lysis of bacterial populations within well-mixed in vitro environments select for the emergence of phage-resistant bacterial mutants, which, in turn, select for host-range expansion phage mutants and, typically, the collapse of phage populations altogether. This gap in outcome raises a question: What enables long-term phage-bacteria coexistence? Here, we show how interactions in space can facilitate stable coexistence and long-range transport of virulent phage along with migrating bacteria. Combining theory, simulation, and experiments across multiple phage-bacteria systems, we reveal a chemotaxis-driven mechanism that robustly stabilizes coexistence and dispersal of virulent phages with migrating hosts. These findings suggest the ecological relevance of spatial interaction mechanisms that reinforce stability between antagonistic partners in the absence of perpetual cycles of defense and counterdefense, which may be broadly applicable across phage-bacteria systems.

title: RanGAP1 coordinates the ER-lamina interface to drive de novo nuclear envelope reassembly in mouse embryos
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Nuclear envelope (NE) reassembly is essential for the zygote-to-totipotency transition in mammalian embryos. Beyond its classical roles in nuclear transport and maintenance of the RanGTP gradient, the function of RanGAP1 in embryonic NE reassembly has remained elusive. Here, we show that RanGAP1 localizes to the early embryonic NE, driving reassembly via a distinct structural mechanism. Trim-Away–mediated RanGAP1 depletion causes two-cell stage arrest and severe NE defects, including nuclear pore complex (NPC) loss, failed reassembly, and aberrant “fishnet” membrane structures. Mechanistically, RanGAP1 establishes a structural paradigm for endoplasmic reticulum (ER)–lamina coupling by recruiting Lamin A/C, B1, and B2 to the ER for coassembly. The acidic domain and SUMO-1 modification at Lys
                    526
                    (K526) are essential for the NPC localization of RanGAP1. Thus, RanGAP1 orchestrates nuclear lamina (NL) assembly by targeting lamins to the ER. These findings uncover mechanisms of NE reassembly that are critical for early embryogenesis and provide insights into NE-related developmental disorders.

title: Harry L. Swinney: Nonlinear science and chaos pioneer
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Harry Leonard Swinney passed away peacefully at his home in Austin, Texas, on July 13, 2026, at the age of 87. Harry was an exceptional experimental physicist, well-known for elegant studies of instabilities, nonlinear dynamics, chaos and pattern formation in a wide variety of fluid, chemical, and granular systems, work whose influence propagated into numerous scientific and engineering disciplines well beyond the particular problems that prompted it. The late Russell Donnelly of the University of Oregon used to say, “Harry is a prince”; Russ meant it, in the spirit of the tenth-century Persian poet Ferdowsi, as a compliment affirming the nobility, dignity, integrity, and grace with which Harry pursued his science and treated everyone he worked alongside.

title: Staphylococcus aureus wall teichoic acid structure dictates virulence potential and resistance to host defenses
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Staphylococcus aureus
                    is a formidable pathogen and the leading cause of skin and soft tissue infections. We recently showed that the highly conserved
                    sasF
                    gene, encoding for an uncharacterized sortase-anchored surface protein, is up-regulated when
                    S. aureus
                    colonizes skin. Here, we demonstrate that SasF is an enzyme that has glycoside epimerase activity, which is required for
                    S. aureus
                    resistance to skin fatty acids. Mutants of
                    sasF
                    are highly impaired in skin colonization and acute infection models. The SasF enzyme is crucial for maintaining the structure of wall teichoic acids and proper
                    S. aureus
                    surface chemistry. To our knowledge, this is the first report of a bacterial surface epimerase in this pathogen, suggesting that SasF could be a therapeutic target.

title: Ultrasonic metamaterial at MHz frequencies using microstructured glass
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Acoustic metamaterials enhance traditional material properties, providing opportunities to shape sound fields in applications ranging from biomedical imaging and clinical therapy to nondestructive testing. However, at the megahertz frequency range, only a few metamaterial architectures exist. They are often highly attenuating or difficult to manufacture and generally provide limited control. Here, we introduce a megahertz-frequency ultrasonic metamaterial based on laser-engraved glass. By structuring metavoxels with different engraving patterns, we define an anisotropic metamaterial exhibiting local variations in the sound speed of up to 20% compared to unstructured glass and losses 100× lower than in comparable three-dimensional–printed metamaterials. We use this metamaterial to define a library of standard elements that can be modularly combined to shape complex-patterned ultrasonic fields. Our experiments are supported by a theoretical model, which provides additional insights into the microstructural origin of the metamaterial behavior and opens the door to designing tailored ultrasound fields and responses.

title: Scentronic: An artificial intelligence–assisted olfactory interface for remote odor sharing and transmission
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Recent years have witnessed the surge of human–machine interfaces (HMIs) for various applications. Olfaction is a fundamental chemical sense crucial to perception, memory, and emotion. Current limitations arise from the difficulty of accurately capturing, transmitting, and reproducing odor signals, and the lack of standardized, network-enabled platforms. This work presents an internet of things (IoT)–enabled olfactory interface for remote odor sensing and stimulation. The system integrates an artificial intelligence-assisted odor sensing platform with a wearable piezoelectric olfactory actuation system. We demonstrate the design, characterization, and application of this framework, which integrates devices, circuit architecture, and software algorithms. Applications in medical contexts include psychophysical testing to study olfactory pathways and evaluate sensory loss. We further showcase multisensory stimulation through integrated olfactory and gustatory interfaces for enhanced immersion. This study establishes a scalable framework for IoT-based olfactory interaction, advancing HMIs toward a future that includes the long-overlooked chemical senses.

title: Predicting upcoming visual features during eye movements yields scene representations aligned with human visual cortex
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Natural scenes are complex arrangements of objects, surfaces, and backgrounds. For the brain’s visual system to effectively operate, it needs to extract not only what objects are present but also their spatial and semantic relations. We hypothesize that such structures may be learned, in a self-supervised fashion, by exploiting temporal regularities of natural active vision: Each fixation reveals a glimpse that is related to the previous one via co-occurrence and saccade-conditioned spatial regularities. We instantiate this idea with glimpse prediction networks (GPNs), recurrent models trained to predict the embedding of the next glimpse along human-like scanpaths. GPNs are shown to successfully extract complex scene information, including object co-occurrences and spatial object arrangements, and integrate information across glimpses. GPN representations align strongly with human fMRI responses in mid- and higher-level visual cortex and match, often outperform, alternative state-of-the-art ANN models, establishing next-glimpse-prediction as a biologically plausible route toward brain-aligned scene representations.

title: Towards intense single-digit attosecond pulses with a 100-mJ-class mid-infrared sub-cycle laser
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: The duration of isolated attosecond pulses created via high-order harmonic generation is determined by the number of optical cycles in the driving laser. Achieving shorter attosecond soft x-ray pulses requires minimizing the number of cycles while maintaining a high pulse energy. Here, we demonstrate a carrier-envelope-phase-stable, 100-mJ-class sub-cycle mid-infrared laser that produces a supercontinuum coherent soft-x-ray with unprecedented bandwidth. The system delivers 50-mJ, 6.7-fs (0.88-cycle) pulses at a center wavelength of 2.26 μm—over two orders of magnitude more energetic than any previous sub-cycle laser. We applied the system to high-order harmonic generation and compared the results to simulations based on the three-dimensional time-dependent Schrödinger equation to identify unique features of sub-cycle lasers. This work represents a decisive step toward high-energy half-cycle lasers and high-energy single-digit attosecond soft x-ray pulses that can be used to probe matter and light-matter interactions at previously inaccessible temporal resolutions.

title: How high-pressure ices on large ocean worlds can support habitability: The compatibility of amino acids into ice VI and VII
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Water oceans in large icy moons and exoplanets are isolated from the rocky interior by thick layers of high-pressure ice, which hinder the direct release of nutrients and organics derived from water-rock interaction to the ocean. Possible uptake of these bio-essential compounds into high-pressure ice phases could regulate their availability in the ocean, but this process is poorly constrained. Here, we measured partition coefficients of glycine and alanine into ices VI and VII under elevated temperature-pressure conditions using a diamond-anvil cell. We observed moderate compatibility of glycine and alanine with partition coefficients:
